items.name: Tomatoes, Whole or Halved
items.safety_notes: Must acidify: 2 tbsp bottled lemon juice or ½ tsp citric acid per pint (double for quarts). Do not use fresh lemon juice.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 21 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 13 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 53 pounds and yields 15 to 21 quarts — an average of 3 pounds per quart.
tips: Buy a full bushel if processing 7-quart loads repeatedly.
Weigh tomatoes before starting; yield varies by meatiness.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only disease-free, preferably vine-ripened, firm tomatoes. Caution: Do not can tomatoes from dead or frost-killed vines. Green tomatoes are more acidic than ripened fruit and can be canned safely. Overripe tomatoes may have lower acidity and should be avoided.
tips: Discard any tomatoes with signs of rot, mold, or decay.
Roma (paste) tomatoes give meatier packs with less liquid.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash tomatoes and dip in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds or until skins crack. Then dip in cold water, slip off skins, and remove cores. Leave whole or halve. Add bottled lemon juice or citric acid to jars (see Acid Addition). Add 1 teaspoon of salt per quart to the jars, if desired.
tips: Use a sharp paring knife to core after peeling.
Keep peeled tomatoes in acidulated water to prevent browning.
Do not skip acid addition — tomato pH can exceed 4.6.

sections.heading: Acid Addition
sections.body: To ensure safe acidity in whole, crushed, or juiced tomatoes, add 2 tablespoons of bottled lemon juice or 1/2 teaspoon of citric acid per quart of tomatoes. For pints, use 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice or 1/4 teaspoon citric acid. Acid can be added directly to each jar before filling with product. Add sugar to offset acid taste, if desired. Four tablespoons of 5-percent-acidity vinegar per quart may be used instead of lemon juice or citric acid. However, vinegar may cause undesirable flavor changes.
tips: Use bottled lemon juice, not fresh — acidity is standardized.
Add acid before filling jars, not after.

sections.heading: Procedure — Raw Pack
sections.body: Add acid to jars (see Acid Addition). Fill jars with raw tomatoes, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Press tomatoes in the jars until spaces between them fill with juice. Leave 1/2-inch headspace. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Pack tomatoes snugly but do not crush them.
Raw pack yields a firmer, less broken-down product.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Add acid to jars (see Acid Addition). Heat tomatoes slowly. Place tomatoes in a large saucepan; add enough water to cover, and boil gently for 5 minutes. Fill jars with hot tomatoes and cooking liquid, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Hot pack allows tighter packing and fewer floating pieces.
Skim foam before filling jars.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time as follows: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min. Dial-Gauge Pressure Canner — at 2,001–4,000 ft use 11 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft use 12 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft use 13 lb; 8,001–10,000 ft use 14 lb. Weighted-Gauge Pressure Canner — above 1,000 ft use 15 lb weight.
tips: Always know your altitude before selecting processing time.
Dial gauges must be tested annually for accuracy.

items.name: Tomatoes, Crushed
items.safety_notes: Must acidify: 2 tbsp bottled lemon juice or ½ tsp citric acid per pint (double for quarts).

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 22 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 14 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 53 pounds and yields 17 to 20 quarts — an average of about 2-3/4 pounds per quart.
tips: Use meaty, low-moisture tomatoes for the best crushed texture.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only disease-free, preferably vine-ripened, firm tomatoes. Do not can tomatoes from dead or frost-killed vines.
tips: Avoid overripe or very soft tomatoes — they yield a watery product.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash tomatoes. Dip in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds or until skins crack. Dip in cold water, slip off skins, and remove cores. Trim off any bruised or discolored portions and quarter. Heat 1/6 of the quarters quickly in a large pot, crushing them with a wooden mallet or spoon as they are added to the pot. This prevents separation. Continue to slowly add and crush remaining tomatoes. Stir frequently. Boil gently for 5 minutes after all tomatoes are added. Add bottled lemon juice or citric acid to jars (see Acid Addition). Add 1 teaspoon salt per quart, if desired. Fill jars immediately with hot crushed tomatoes, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Heat the first batch quickly to inactivate pectinase and prevent juice/pulp separation.
Stir constantly once boiling to prevent scorching.
Fill jars immediately — crushed tomatoes thicken quickly.

sections.heading: Acid Addition
sections.body: Add 2 tablespoons of bottled lemon juice or 1/2 teaspoon of citric acid per quart. For pints, use 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice or 1/4 teaspoon citric acid. Add acid directly to each jar before filling.
tips: Use bottled lemon juice for consistent acidity.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min. Dial-Gauge Pressure Canner — 2,001–4,000 ft use 11 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft use 12 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft use 13 lb; 8,001–10,000 ft use 14 lb. Weighted-Gauge — above 1,000 ft use 15 lb weight.
tips: Altitude adjustments apply to both water bath and pressure methods.

items.name: Tomato Juice
items.safety_notes: Must acidify: 2 tbsp bottled lemon juice or ½ tsp citric acid per pint.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 23 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 14 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 53 pounds and yields 15 to 18 quarts of juice — an average of 3-1/2 pounds per quart.
tips: Juicing tomatoes with a food mill removes seeds and skins efficiently.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only disease-free, preferably vine-ripened, firm tomatoes. Do not use tomatoes from dead or frost-killed vines.
tips: Choose fully ripe, deep-red tomatoes for the richest juice color and flavor.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash tomatoes. Dip in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds or until skins crack. Dip in cold water and slip off skins. Remove cores and any bruised or discolored portions. Quarter tomatoes into a large saucepan. Crush, heat, and simmer for 5 minutes before juicing. Strain hot mixture through a sieve or food mill to remove skins and seeds. Add bottled lemon juice or citric acid to jars (see Acid Addition). Add 1 teaspoon salt per quart, if desired. Reheat juice to boiling. Fill jars with hot juice, leaving 1/4-inch headspace. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Heat quickly at the start to prevent juice/pulp separation.
Do not add water — tomatoes provide sufficient liquid.
A food mill makes straining quick and keeps seeds out.

sections.heading: Acid Addition
sections.body: Add 2 tablespoons of bottled lemon juice or 1/2 teaspoon of citric acid per quart. For pints, use 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice or 1/4 teaspoon citric acid. Add acid to jars before filling with hot juice.
tips: Never omit the acid step for tomato juice.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min. Dial-Gauge Pressure Canner — 2,001–4,000 ft use 11 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft use 12 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft use 13 lb; 8,001–10,000 ft use 14 lb. Weighted-Gauge — above 1,000 ft use 15 lb weight.

items.name: Tomato Sauce
items.safety_notes: Must acidify: 2 tbsp bottled lemon juice or ½ tsp citric acid per pint.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: For thin sauce, an average of 35 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; 21 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. For thick sauce, an average of 46 pounds is needed per 7-quart load; 28 pounds per 9-pint load. A bushel weighs 53 pounds and yields 10 to 12 quarts of thin sauce or 7 to 9 quarts of thick sauce.
tips: Start with more tomatoes than you think you need — significant volume is lost during cooking.
Roma tomatoes yield a thicker sauce with less cooking time.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only disease-free, preferably vine-ripened, firm tomatoes. Do not can tomatoes from dead or frost-killed vines.
tips: Paste-type tomatoes (Roma, San Marzano) are ideal for sauce.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Prepare and press as for tomato juice. Simmer in a large-diameter saucepan until sauce reaches desired consistency. Boil until volume is reduced by about one-third for thin sauce or one-half for thick sauce. Add bottled lemon juice or citric acid to jars (see Acid Addition). Add 1 teaspoon salt per quart, if desired. Fill jars with hot sauce, leaving 1/4-inch headspace. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Use a wide, shallow pan to speed evaporation and thickening.
Stir frequently during reduction to prevent scorching.
Measure volume periodically to track reduction progress.

sections.heading: Acid Addition
sections.body: Add 2 tablespoons of bottled lemon juice or 1/2 teaspoon of citric acid per quart. For pints, use 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice or 1/4 teaspoon citric acid. Add acid to each jar before filling with sauce.
tips: Acid is required regardless of how thick the sauce is reduced.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min. Dial-Gauge Pressure Canner — 2,001–4,000 ft use 11 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft use 12 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft use 13 lb; 8,001–10,000 ft use 14 lb. Weighted-Gauge — above 1,000 ft use 15 lb weight.

items.name: Tomato Salsa
items.safety_notes: Use only a USDA-tested recipe. Do not alter vegetable or vinegar proportions.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: The tested USDA/NCHFP recipe for tomato salsa yields approximately 16 to 18 pints. Typical ingredients include 7 quarts (about 22 lbs) of peeled, cored, chopped tomatoes, 4 cups seeded chopped long green peppers, 5 cups chopped onion, 1/2 cup seeded chopped jalapeño peppers, 6 cloves minced garlic, 2 cups bottled lemon or lime juice, 2 tablespoons salt, 1 tablespoon black pepper, and 2 tablespoons fresh or dried oregano (optional), and 1 tablespoon fresh cilantro (optional).
tips: Do not reduce the proportion of acid or increase low-acid vegetables.
Wear gloves when handling hot peppers.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only tested, approved salsa recipes for home canning. The proportions of vegetables, especially low-acid ones like peppers and onions, are critical to safety. Do not alter the ratio of low-acid to high-acid ingredients. Use firm, ripe tomatoes — meaty varieties such as Roma are preferred.
tips: Never substitute low-acid ingredients for tomatoes — this changes the pH.
Fresh herbs are for flavor only; do not increase their quantity for safety.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Caution: Do not alter the proportions of vegetables or omit acid. Wash and prepare vegetables as directed. Combine all ingredients in a large saucepan. Heat, stirring frequently, until mixture boils. Reduce heat and simmer for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally. Ladle hot salsa into hot pint jars, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles and adjust headspace if needed. Wipe jar rims. Adjust lids and process in a boiling water canner.
tips: Process pints only — quart jars have not been tested for salsa.
Remove air bubbles with a non-metallic spatula after filling.
Label jars with batch date; color changes are normal within 6 months.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.
tips: Salsa is water-bath canned only — do not use pressure canner.

items.name: Tomato Paste
items.safety_notes: Must acidify each jar: 1 tbsp bottled lemon juice or ¼ tsp citric acid per half-pint; 2 tbsp lemon juice or ½ tsp citric acid per pint. Use only ripe, meaty tomatoes.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 22 pounds of tomatoes is needed per canner load of 9 half-pints (8 oz jars). A bushel (53 lbs) yields about 10 to 11 half-pints of paste.
tips: Paste-type tomatoes (Roma, San Marzano) are strongly preferred.
Expect dramatic volume reduction — paste is very concentrated.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only disease-free, preferably vine-ripened, firm tomatoes. Paste tomatoes with low water content produce the thickest paste in the shortest cooking time.
tips: Split and taste tomatoes before using — bitter fruit makes bitter paste.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash tomatoes, dip in boiling water to crack skins, cool, peel, core, and quarter. Simmer until soft and press through a sieve or food mill. Add 1 bay leaf and 1 medium sweet red pepper (optional) per 4 cups pulp. Continue simmering, stirring frequently to prevent burning, until paste mounds up on a spoon without free liquid separating out. Remove bay leaf. Add 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice per half-pint jar. Fill hot half-pint jars with hot paste, leaving 1/4-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Use a heavy-bottomed pot and very low heat during final reduction.
Stir every 5 minutes once paste is thick to prevent scorching.
Half-pint jars are the tested size — do not use larger jars.

sections.heading: Acid Addition
sections.body: Add 1 tablespoon of bottled lemon juice per half-pint jar to ensure safe acidity. Add acid to each jar before filling with paste.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Spaghetti Sauce (Without Meat)
items.safety_notes: Must acidify: 2 tbsp bottled lemon juice or ½ tsp citric acid per pint (double for quarts). Use only tested recipe — do not alter proportions of low-acid vegetables.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: The tested USDA recipe yields approximately 9 pints. Typical ingredients include 30 lbs tomatoes, 1 cup chopped onion, 5 cloves garlic, 1 cup seeded and chopped green pepper, 1 lb sliced fresh mushrooms (optional), 4-1/2 teaspoons salt, 2 tablespoons oregano, 4 tablespoons minced fresh parsley, 2 teaspoons black pepper, 1/4 cup brown sugar, and 1/4 cup vegetable oil.
tips: Do not increase low-acid vegetables beyond tested proportions.
Oil must not be increased — it affects heat penetration.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only disease-free, vine-ripened, firm tomatoes. The tested recipe relies on a specific ratio of tomatoes to low-acid ingredients to maintain safe pH. Do not substitute or increase the amounts of onion, peppers, garlic, or mushrooms.
tips: Fresh mushrooms may be omitted but not increased.
Do not add meat — a separate tested meat-sauce recipe must be used.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Caution: Do not increase the proportion of onions, peppers, or mushrooms. Wash tomatoes and dip in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds until skins crack; dip in cold water and slip off skins. Core and quarter. Boil 20 minutes, uncovered, in a large saucepan. Press through a food mill or fine sieve. Sauté onions, garlic, and peppers in oil until tender. Combine with tomato pulp. Add remaining ingredients except mushrooms. Bring to a boil and simmer uncovered, stirring frequently, until thick enough for serving (about 1 hour). Add mushrooms and simmer 30 minutes. Add bottled lemon juice or citric acid to jars. Fill jars with hot sauce, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Sauté vegetables before adding to sauce for better flavor.
Simmer uncovered to allow evaporation and thickening.
Use 1-inch headspace (not the typical 1/4 inch) for this sauce.

sections.heading: Acid Addition
sections.body: Add bottled lemon juice or citric acid to each jar before filling: 2 tablespoons bottled lemon juice or 1/2 teaspoon citric acid per quart; 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice or 1/4 teaspoon citric acid per pint.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.
tips: Process pints for 35 min and quarts for 40 min at sea level (water bath).

items.name: Ketchup
items.safety_notes: Use only a tested recipe. Do not reduce vinegar or alter proportions. Acidification is provided by the vinegar in tested recipes.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: The USDA tested recipe yields 6 to 7 pints. Typical ingredients include 24 lbs ripe tomatoes, 3 cups chopped onion, 3/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper, 3 cups cider vinegar (5% acidity), 1-1/2 teaspoons whole cloves, 3 sticks cinnamon, 1-1/2 teaspoons whole allspice, 3 tablespoons celery seeds, 1-1/2 cups sugar, and 1/4 cup canning salt.
tips: Use only 5%-acidity cider vinegar — do not substitute.
Use a spice bag for whole spices to make removal easy.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only disease-free, vine-ripened, firm, ripe red tomatoes. Soft or overripe tomatoes yield a thin, watery ketchup.
tips: Meaty paste tomatoes produce a richer, more concentrated ketchup.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash tomatoes, core, peel, and quarter. Combine tomatoes, onions, and cayenne in a large saucepan. Bring to a boil and simmer 20 minutes. Press through a food mill; discard skins and seeds. Combine vinegar and spices in a separate saucepan. Bring to a boil and simmer 20 minutes; strain spices out and add spiced vinegar to tomato mixture. Add sugar and salt. Boil mixture rapidly, stirring frequently, until volume is reduced by one-half (may take 1 to 2 hours). As mixture thickens, stir frequently to prevent scorching. Fill pint or half-pint jars with hot ketchup, leaving 1/8-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Reduce heat as mixture thickens to avoid scorching.
Use a wide, heavy-bottomed pot for even heat distribution.
Skim foam during the final reduction phase.
1/8-inch headspace is correct for ketchup — very tight fit.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Green Beans
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning is required — water bath canning is unsafe.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 14 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 9 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 30 pounds and yields 12 to 20 quarts — an average of 2 pounds per quart.
tips: Buy or pick beans the same day you plan to can them for best quality.
Beans lose quality quickly after harvest — refrigerate if there is any delay.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select filled but tender, crisp pods. Remove and discard any diseased and rusty pods. Wash beans and trim ends. Leave whole, cut in 2-inch pieces, or snap.
tips: Avoid over-mature beans with tough, fibrous pods.
Discard any pods with brown spots, rust, or mold.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash beans and trim ends. Leave whole, cut in 2-inch pieces, or snap. If desired, add 1/2 teaspoon of salt per pint jar or 1 teaspoon per quart jar. Salt is optional and used for flavor only — it is not required for safety.
tips: Use canning or pickling salt only — table salt with iodine may cause discoloration.
Snap beans into uniform pieces so they pack and heat evenly.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Cover beans with boiling water; boil 5 minutes. Fill jars loosely with beans, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1/2 teaspoon salt per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart if desired. Cover with hot cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe jar rims. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Pack loosely — over-packing inhibits heat penetration.
Use the cooking liquid to fill jars, not plain water, to retain flavor.

sections.heading: Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars tightly with raw beans, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1/2 teaspoon salt per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart if desired. Add boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe jar rims. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Pack raw beans tightly — they will shrink during processing.
Ensure boiling water fully covers beans before closing the lid.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only. Water bath canning is NOT safe for green beans — they are a low-acid food and can harbor Clostridium botulinum spores that survive boiling-water temperatures. See the processing table for times: pints 20 minutes, quarts 25 minutes at 10 lb weighted-gauge pressure or 11 lb dial-gauge pressure (at 0–2,000 ft altitude).
tips: Never attempt to water-bath can green beans — botulism risk is severe.
Vent the canner for 10 minutes before closing the petcock or weighted gauge.
Allow pressure to drop naturally — do not rush the depressurization.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Have your dial gauge tested for accuracy annually at your local cooperative extension office.

items.name: Corn, Whole Kernel
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 31.5 pounds (in husk) is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 20 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 35 pounds and yields 6 to 11 quarts — an average of 4.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Process corn the same day it is harvested — sugar converts to starch within hours.
Pick or buy corn when kernels are at the milk stage for best flavor.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select ears with fresh husks, plump milky kernels, and thin skin (tough skin indicates over-maturity). Reject corn with dried or doughy kernels.
tips: Pierce a kernel with a fingernail — it should release a milky liquid, not water or paste.
Use corn within 6–8 hours of picking for peak sweetness.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Husk corn and remove silk. Wash ears. Cut kernels from cob at three-quarters of kernel depth. Do not scrape cob. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: Cut kernels off the cob into a large bowl to contain splatter.
Do not scrape the cob — scraping adds starchy liquid that thickens the pack and impedes heat penetration.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Add 1 cup of hot water per 4 cups of kernels. Bring to a boil, reduce heat, and simmer 5 minutes. Fill jars with corn and cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Stir corn and water together before heating to distribute starch evenly.

sections.heading: Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with raw kernels, leaving 1-inch headspace. Do not shake or press down. Add boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Do not pack raw corn too tightly — leave room for liquid to circulate.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — corn is a low-acid vegetable and water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 55 minutes. Quarts: 85 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: The long processing time for corn is necessary — do not shorten it.
Allow the canner to depressurize completely before opening (may take 30–45 minutes).

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Do not increase processing time to compensate for altitude — increase pressure as directed.

items.name: Corn, Cream Style
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required. Pints ONLY — do not process quarts. Cream-style corn is too dense for safe heat penetration in quart jars.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 20 pounds (in husk) is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 35 pounds and yields about 12 to 20 pints. PINTS ONLY — do not process cream-style corn in quart jars.
tips: Plan for approximately 3–4 ears of corn per pint jar.
Cream-style corn must be processed in pints only — the dense product does not heat safely in quarts.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select ears with fresh husks, plump milky kernels, and thin skin. Over-mature corn with tough, doughy kernels produces inferior cream-style product.
tips: Milk-stage corn (kernels release milky juice when pierced) is essential for cream-style.
Process immediately after harvest — corn starch converts quickly.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Husk and remove silk. Wash ears. Cut kernels from the cob at one-half the depth of the kernels. Then scrape the remaining kernel portions and milk from the cob with the back of a knife blade to produce the 'cream' component. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint.
tips: The two-step cut-then-scrape method is what distinguishes cream-style from whole kernel.
Use a bundt pan or bowl to stabilize the ear while cutting.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Combine corn with 1 cup of boiling water per quart of corn. Heat to boiling. Fill pint jars with hot corn mixture, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. HOT PACK ONLY for cream-style corn.
tips: Raw pack is not recommended for cream-style corn — always use hot pack.
The mixture will be thick; use a wide-mouth funnel to fill jars cleanly.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process only in a pressure canner. PINTS ONLY: 85 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft). Water bath canning is not safe for this product.
tips: 85 minutes is the full required time — do not reduce it.
Use only pint jars — quart jars of cream-style corn are not safe to process.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Altitude affects pressure requirements, not processing time — keep time at 85 minutes regardless of elevation.

items.name: Carrots
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 17.5 pounds (without tops) is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 11 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 50 pounds and yields 17 to 25 quarts — an average of 2.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Choose slender carrots (1 to 1.25 inches in diameter) for best texture after canning.
Remove tops immediately after harvest to prevent moisture loss.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select small to medium carrots, preferably 1 to 1.25 inches in diameter. Larger carrots may be fibrous and less flavorful. Wash, peel, and rewash carrots. Slice or dice into 1/2-inch pieces, leave whole if small.
tips: Avoid cracked, over-mature, or woody carrots.
Baby-cut carrots from the store may be used but give a less traditional result.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash, peel, and rewash carrots. Slice or dice into pieces no more than 1/2 inch thick. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon of canning salt per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: Peel carrots thoroughly — the skin can harbor soil bacteria.
Uniform pieces ensure even heat penetration during processing.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Cover carrots with boiling water and boil 5 minutes. Fill jars with carrots, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Cover with hot cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Reserve and use the cooking liquid to fill jars for better flavor and color.

sections.heading: Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars tightly with raw carrots, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Add boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Pack tightly — carrots shrink slightly during processing.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — carrots are a low-acid vegetable and water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 25 minutes. Quarts: 30 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Never water-bath can plain carrots.
For canned pickled carrots, see the Pickled Dilled Carrots recipe (water bath is then acceptable).

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: At elevations above 1,000 ft, switch the weighted gauge from 10 lb to 15 lb.

items.name: Beets
items.safety_notes: Low-acid. Pressure canning required. For a water bath option, see Pickled Beets.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 21 pounds (without tops) is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 13.5 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 52 pounds and yields 15 to 24 quarts — an average of 2.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Choose beets 1 to 2 inches in diameter for best texture — large beets tend to be fibrous.
Leave 2 inches of tap root and 1 inch of stem on beets before cooking to prevent color bleeding.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select small beets 1 to 2 inches in diameter. Larger beets are often fibrous and less sweet. Trim tops, leaving 1 inch of stem and taproot attached. Wash thoroughly.
tips: Very large beets (over 3 inches) should be reserved for pickling or fresh use — they don't can as well.
Golden and Chioggia beet varieties can be canned using the same procedure.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Trim off beet tops, leaving 1 inch of the stem and taproot to prevent color loss. Wash thoroughly. Sort by size for uniform cooking. Boil in water until skins slip easily — small beets 15 to 25 minutes, medium beets 25 to 30 minutes. Cool in cold water. Trim roots and stems and slip off skins. Leave small beets whole; halve or quarter medium beets. Slice or cube if desired. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: Wear gloves when handling cooked beets to avoid staining hands.
Do not overcook beets before canning — just cook until skins slip.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with hot beets, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Add fresh boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. (Do not use the beet cooking liquid — it is too dark and may affect color.) Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. HOT PACK ONLY for beets.
tips: Use fresh boiling water, not the beet cooking water, to fill jars.
Pack beets tightly — they do not expand significantly during processing.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — beets are a low-acid vegetable. Water bath canning is not safe for plain beets; for a water-bath option, see Pickled Beets. Pints: 30 minutes. Quarts: 35 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Beets require hot pack only — do not raw pack.
If you want to water-bath can beets, use the Pickled Beets recipe with vinegar.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Processing time stays the same at all altitudes — only pressure changes.

items.name: Potatoes, Cubed
items.safety_notes: Low-acid. Pressure canning required. Cut into 1-inch cubes.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 35 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 21 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 50 pounds and yields 15 to 20 quarts — an average of 2.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Use mature, freshly dug potatoes for best results.
New potatoes are ideal — they hold their shape better than old potatoes.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select small to medium potatoes, 2 to 3 inches in diameter. Wash and peel. Cut into 1-inch cubes. To prevent browning, keep cut potatoes in water during preparation. Drain, cook in fresh water, and proceed.
tips: Do not use old, sprouting, or green-tinged potatoes.
Soak cut potatoes in cold water to prevent discoloration before blanching.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash and peel potatoes. Cut into 1-inch cubes. To prevent darkening, hold cut potatoes in cold water. Drain, cover with fresh boiling water, boil 2 minutes, and drain again before packing jars. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: The pre-boil step removes excess starch that can clog the jar and impede heat penetration.
Do not skip the drain-and-fresh-water step — using the starchy soak water reduces quality.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: After the preliminary boil, fill jars with hot potatoes, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Cover with fresh hot boiling water (not the cooking water), leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. HOT PACK ONLY for cubed potatoes.
tips: Use fresh boiling water to fill jars, not the potato cooking liquid.
Leave exactly 1-inch headspace — potatoes expand during processing.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — potatoes are a low-acid vegetable and water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 35 minutes. Quarts: 40 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Do not can mashed or pureed potatoes — only cubed or whole small potatoes.
Allow full natural pressure release before opening the canner.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Check your dial gauge for accuracy each canning season.

items.name: Peas, Shelled
items.safety_notes: Low-acid. Pressure canning required. Pints recommended for best quality.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 31.5 pounds (in pods) is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 20 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 30 pounds and yields 5 to 10 quarts — an average of 4.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Shell and process peas the same day they are picked for best sweetness and quality.
Peas deteriorate quickly after harvest — refrigerate immediately if there is any delay.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select filled pods containing young, tender, sweet peas. Discard diseased or insect-damaged pods. Do not use over-mature, tough, or starchy peas.
tips: Taste a raw pea — it should be sweet and tender, not starchy.
Flat or wrinkled pods indicate over-mature peas that will be tough after canning.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Shell and wash peas. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: Rinse shelled peas in cold water to remove any debris from the pods.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Cover peas with boiling water. Bring to a boil and boil 2 minutes. Fill jars loosely with peas, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Cover with hot cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Pack loosely — peas swell during processing and tight packing can prevent adequate heat penetration.

sections.heading: Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with raw peas, leaving 1-inch headspace. Do not shake or press down. Add salt if desired. Add boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Do not pack raw peas tightly — they will expand.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — shelled peas are a low-acid vegetable. Water bath canning is not safe. Pints and quarts: 40 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft). Note: pints are recommended for best quality.
tips: Pints and quarts process for the same time (40 minutes) — unusual among vegetables.
Pints are preferred — they tend to yield a better texture product.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Above 1,000 ft, use the 15 lb weighted gauge regardless of how little above 1,000 ft you are.

items.name: Asparagus
items.safety_notes: Low-acid. Pressure canning required.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 24.5 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 16 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A crate weighs 31 pounds and yields 7 to 12 quarts — an average of 3 pounds per quart.
tips: Process asparagus within 2–3 hours of harvest or purchase for best quality.
Spears continue to toughen after cutting — refrigerate immediately if you can't process right away.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select young, tender, tight-tipped spears. Wash thoroughly and cut off and discard any tough white scales. Trim ends and wash again. Spears can be left whole (to fit jar height) or cut into 1-inch pieces.
tips: Spears with loose or flowering tips are over-mature — avoid them.
Medium-diameter spears (pencil to finger thickness) can best evenly.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash asparagus thoroughly and cut off tough white scales. Trim tough ends. Leave in spear form to pack upright, or cut into 1-inch pieces. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: For whole spears, measure jar height and cut spears to fit with 1-inch headspace.
Cut tips from some spears to fit in the gaps when packing whole spears.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Cover spears or pieces with boiling water. Boil 2 to 3 minutes. Loosely fill jars with hot asparagus, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Cover with hot cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Pack spears tip-end up in wide-mouth jars for an attractive presentation.

sections.heading: Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars tightly with raw spears, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Add boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Pack raw spears tightly — they shrink noticeably during processing.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — asparagus is a low-acid vegetable. Water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 30 minutes. Quarts: 40 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Never water-bath can asparagus — for a water-bath option, see Pickled Asparagus.
Quarts require 10 more minutes than pints — do not use pint times for quarts.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Processing time does not change with altitude — adjust only the pressure.

items.name: Winter Squash / Pumpkin
items.safety_notes: Low-acid. Must be cubed — do not mash or purée for canning. Pressure canning required.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 16 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 10 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. Yield varies greatly by variety; a typical 10-pound pumpkin yields about 5 quarts of cubed product.
tips: This procedure applies to butternut, acorn, Hubbard, banana squash, and sugar/pie pumpkins.
Decorative carving pumpkins (jack-o-lantern types) are too watery and stringy — use sugar or pie pumpkins.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, mature squash or pumpkins with hard rinds and stringless, mature pulp. Small sugar or pie pumpkins are better for canning than large carving pumpkins, which are too watery and stringy. Remove seeds, peel, and cut into 1-inch cubes.
tips: Avoid squash with soft spots, mold, or damaged rinds.
Do not can green, immature squash — it must be fully cured and hard-rinded.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash squash. Remove seeds. Peel and cut flesh into 1-inch cubes. CRITICAL: Do not mash or puree squash for home canning — only cubed pieces are tested and safe. Pureed squash is too dense for adequate heat penetration. Salt is not typically added to squash.
tips: A sturdy vegetable peeler or paring knife works well for peeling hard squash.
Cube pieces as uniformly as possible — 1-inch cubes heat most evenly.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Boil cubes in water for 2 minutes. Drain, fill jars with hot cubes, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1/2 teaspoon salt per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart if desired. Cover with fresh boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. HOT PACK ONLY for winter squash and pumpkin.
tips: Use fresh boiling water to fill jars, not the blanching water.
Squash cubes will soften considerably during processing — do not be alarmed.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — winter squash and pumpkin are low-acid vegetables. Water bath canning is not safe. Do not mash or puree. Pints: 55 minutes. Quarts: 90 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Canned squash cubes can be mashed or pureed AFTER opening the jar — just not before canning.
The 90-minute quart time is one of the longest in vegetable canning — plan your day accordingly.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: At high altitude, use the 15 lb weighted-gauge setting above 1,000 ft.

items.name: Beans, Lima / Butter (Shelled)
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required. Do not pack tightly — fill loosely to allow adequate heat penetration.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 32 pounds (in pods) is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 21 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 32 pounds and yields 6 to 10 quarts of shelled beans — an average of 5 pounds per quart.
tips: Shell lima beans just before processing — shelled beans deteriorate quickly.
A bushel in the pod yields far fewer shelled beans than expected — plan quantities carefully.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select well-filled pods with green seeds. Discard insect-damaged pods or seeds. Shell beans and discard any that are shriveled, discolored, or over-mature (hard and starchy). Wash shelled beans thoroughly.
tips: Beans with a white or dry appearance are over-mature and will be mealy after canning.
Young, bright-green beans produce the best canned product.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Shell and wash beans. For small beans, leave whole. Do not pack tightly — the USDA specifies loosely packed jars for adequate heat penetration. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: Do NOT pack lima beans tightly — loose packing is critical for safe heat penetration.
Use wide-mouth jars if available — easier to fill and empty.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Cover beans with boiling water. Boil 3 minutes. Loosely fill jars with beans and cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace for small beans, 1.5 inches for large beans. Add salt if desired. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Leave extra headspace (1.5 inches) for large lima beans — they expand more.

sections.heading: Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars loosely with raw beans, leaving 1-inch headspace for small beans, 1.5 inches for large beans. Do not press or shake down. Add salt if desired. Add boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Loose packing is especially important for raw pack — never tamp down lima beans.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — lima beans are a low-acid vegetable. Water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 40 minutes. Quarts: 50 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Lima beans expand significantly — do not overfill jars.
Loose packing in the jar (not tight) is a USDA safety requirement for this vegetable.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Butter beans and Fordhook limas are processed identically to regular lima beans.

items.name: Okra
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required. Use only young, tender pods.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 11 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 7 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 26 pounds and yields 16 to 18 quarts — an average of about 1.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Okra quality declines rapidly — process within 2–3 days of harvest.
For best results harvest okra when pods are 2 to 4 inches long.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select young, tender okra pods 2 to 4 inches long. Older, larger pods become tough and fibrous. Wash thoroughly and trim stems, but do not cut into the seed cell — leave the cap intact to minimize sliminess.
tips: Pods that snap cleanly are at the right stage; pods that bend are over-mature.
Avoid cutting into the seed cavity when trimming — this reduces the mucilaginous texture.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash okra and trim the stem end to just above the seed cell — do not cut into the pod. Leave pods whole or cut into 1-inch pieces. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: Trim the stem flush with the cap rather than cutting into the body of the pod.
Gloves can help reduce skin irritation from the fine hairs on raw okra.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Cover okra with boiling water and boil 2 minutes. Fill jars with hot okra, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Cover with hot cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. HOT PACK ONLY for plain canned okra.
tips: Use the cooking liquid to fill jars — it contains flavor and helps maintain quality.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — okra is a low-acid vegetable. Water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 25 minutes. Quarts: 40 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Okra pints process in 25 minutes but quarts need 40 minutes — do not mix jar sizes in a canner load without using the longer time.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Processing time is fixed — adjust only the gauge pressure for altitude.

items.name: Peppers, Bell / Sweet
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required. Half-pint jars only — USDA does not recommend pint or quart jars for canned sweet peppers due to density concerns.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 9 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 half-pints. HALF-PINT JARS ONLY — the USDA does not provide tested processing times for pint or quart jars of plain canned sweet peppers due to density and heat-penetration concerns.
tips: Only process sweet peppers in half-pint jars — pints and quarts are not USDA-tested for this product.
For larger quantities of canned peppers, plan multiple canner loads.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, crisp, thick-walled peppers. Wash peppers well. Remove seeds and cores. Cut peppers into quarters, strips, or rings. Half-pint jars hold approximately 3/4 pound of prepared pepper pieces.
tips: Red, yellow, and orange bell peppers can be canned using the same procedure as green.
Thin-walled peppers lack the flesh needed to fill jars properly.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Select and wash firm peppers. Remove core and seeds. Quarter, halve, or cut into strips or rings. Flatten quartered pieces. To loosen skins (optional): blister peppers in a 400°F oven or under a broiler for 6 to 8 minutes until skins blister, then cover with a damp cloth and allow to cool before peeling. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per half-pint.
tips: Skin-on peppers can be canned; roasting and peeling is optional but improves texture.
Work quickly after peeling — blistered peppers cool and become slippery.

sections.heading: Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill half-pint jars with raw pepper pieces, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1/2 teaspoon of canning salt if desired. Add boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. Raw pack is the standard method for sweet peppers.
tips: Pack peppers flat in layers for a neater jar and better use of space.
Do not add vinegar or acid — plain canned peppers are pressure-canned, not pickled.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — sweet peppers are a low-acid vegetable. Water bath canning is not safe for plain canned peppers. HALF-PINTS ONLY: 35 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft). For a water-bath option, see Pickled Sweet Peppers.
tips: For pickled peppers that can be water-bath processed, use the Pickled Sweet Peppers recipe.
35 minutes is required even for the small half-pint size due to the density of pepper flesh.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Only half-pint jars have USDA-tested altitude adjustments for plain sweet peppers.

items.name: Spinach and Other Greens
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required. Pack loosely — do not tamp down. Includes spinach, chard, beet greens, kale, turnip greens, and mustard greens.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 28 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 18 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 18 pounds and yields 3 to 9 quarts — an average of 6 pounds per quart. Greens pack down dramatically.
tips: Expect significant volume reduction — what fills a large pot of fresh greens may yield only a few jars.
This procedure applies to spinach, Swiss chard, beet greens, kale, turnip greens, and mustard greens.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select young, tender leaves. Wash very thoroughly — multiple changes of water are necessary to remove grit. Discard any tough or yellow leaves, wilted greens, or greens with significant insect damage.
tips: Grit in canned greens is a common complaint — wash in at least 3 changes of cold water.
Discard any yellowed or damaged leaves before washing.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash greens very thoroughly, changing water several times to remove all grit. Cut out tough stems and midribs. Place 1 pound of greens at a time in a cheesecloth bag or wire basket and steam 3 to 5 minutes or until just wilted. Add 1/2 teaspoon of salt per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart if desired. Salt is optional.
tips: Steam rather than boil greens for the pre-treatment — boiling leaches out more nutrients and flavor.
Have all greens prepped and steamed before you start packing jars.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: After steaming, fill jars loosely with wilted greens, leaving 1-inch headspace. If desired, add 1/2 teaspoon salt per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart. Add fresh boiling water, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. HOT PACK ONLY for canned greens — raw pack is not recommended.
tips: Pack loosely — do not press or tamp down greens. Tight packing prevents adequate heat penetration.
Use fresh boiling water rather than the steaming water to fill jars.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — greens are low-acid vegetables. Water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 70 minutes. Quarts: 90 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft). Processing times are long due to the dense, compact nature of cooked greens.
tips: The 70- and 90-minute times are mandatory — greens are dense and require full penetration.
Do not compress greens in jars — loose pack is a USDA safety requirement.
Plan for a full-day canning session when doing greens.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Both pint and quart times remain the same at altitude — only increase pressure.

items.name: Sweet Potatoes
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required. Cube or leave in pieces — do NOT mash or purée. Mashed sweet potatoes are not safe to home can due to density.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 17.5 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 11 pounds is needed per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 50 pounds and yields 17 to 25 quarts — an average of 2.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Cure freshly dug sweet potatoes at 80–85°F and 85–90% humidity for 1 week before canning for best flavor.
Store cured sweet potatoes at 55–60°F — they become soft and unusable if refrigerated.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose small to medium sweet potatoes of uniform size. They should be firm, smooth, and free of decay. Avoid chilling sweet potatoes before processing — chilling damages texture. Moist-flesh (orange) varieties such as Beauregard and Jewel are most commonly canned.
tips: Do not refrigerate raw sweet potatoes before canning — cold temperatures cause off-flavors and poor texture.
Both moist (orange) and dry (white/yellow) flesh varieties can be canned using the same procedure.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash sweet potatoes. Boil or steam until partially soft — about 15 to 20 minutes. Remove skins; cut into uniform pieces or leave small potatoes whole. CRITICAL: Do not mash or puree sweet potatoes for home canning. Mashed sweet potatoes are too dense for safe heat penetration and are not a USDA-approved product. Salt is optional.
tips: Boiling or steaming until just partially soft makes peeling easy and helps the pieces hold their shape.
Canned sweet potato pieces can be mashed AFTER opening the jar — just not before or during canning.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with hot sweet potato pieces, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1/2 teaspoon salt per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart if desired. For a syrup pack, cover with boiling water or boiling 2% sugar syrup (3 tablespoons sugar per quart of water), leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process. HOT PACK ONLY — raw pack is not recommended for sweet potatoes.
tips: Either water or light sugar syrup can be used as the fill liquid.
Do not use heavy sugar syrup — it impedes heat penetration.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — sweet potatoes are a low-acid vegetable. Water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 65 minutes. Quarts: 90 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Never can sweet potato puree, butter, or mash — only cubed or whole pieces.
The 65-minute pint time and 90-minute quart time reflect the density of sweet potato flesh.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Pressure adjustments apply equally to the dry and moist pack methods.

items.name: Succotash
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable mixture. Pressure canning required. Use only a USDA-tested recipe.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 6 ears of corn plus 3 pounds of shelled lima beans yields about 7 pints. To fill 7 quarts, use approximately 9 ears of corn and 4.5 pounds of shelled limas. Exact yield depends on the size and ratio of vegetables used.
tips: Prepare corn and lima beans separately before combining to ensure uniform quality.
Use fresh-harvested corn and beans on the same day for best flavor.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select fresh, tender corn at the milk stage and young, well-filled lima bean pods. Both vegetables must be at peak eating quality before canning. Discard any damaged kernels or beans. Wash all produce thoroughly.
tips: Quality of the finished product depends entirely on the quality of both vegetables going in.
Do not use over-mature corn or lima beans — they will be tough and starchy after processing.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Prepare corn: husk, remove silk, wash, and cut kernels from cob at 3/4 depth (do not scrape). Shell and wash lima beans. Combine corn and lima beans in equal parts by volume, or use USDA-recommended proportions. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart.
tips: Cut corn kernels without scraping the cob — scraping adds starch that thickens the liquid and slows heat penetration.
Measure corn and lima beans by volume after preparation for consistent proportions.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Mix equal parts of corn kernels and shelled lima beans. Cover with boiling water. Bring to a boil. Fill jars with hot mixture and cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Stir the mixture before filling to distribute corn and beans evenly between jars.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — succotash is a low-acid vegetable mixture. Water bath canning is not safe. Use only a USDA-tested recipe — do not alter vegetable proportions. Pints: 60 minutes. Quarts: 85 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Succotash requires longer processing than either corn or limas alone due to the combined density.
Do not substitute other vegetables for the corn or lima beans in this tested recipe.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: Altitude pressure adjustments are the same as all other pressure-canned vegetables.

items.name: Turnips and Parsnips
items.safety_notes: Low-acid vegetable. Pressure canning required. Use only young, tender roots.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 21 pounds of turnips is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 13 pounds for 9 pints. Parsnip yields are similar. A bushel of turnips weighs 50 pounds and yields 17 to 25 quarts — an average of 2.5 pounds per quart.
tips: Choose turnips or parsnips harvested after the first frost — frost converts starches to sugar and significantly improves flavor.
Small to medium roots (1.5 to 2 inches diameter) yield the best texture after canning.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select young, tender, firm roots that have not been exposed to hard freezes after harvest. Avoid large, fibrous roots or those with hollow centers. Wash thoroughly, trim ends, and peel. Cut into 1/2-inch cubes or 1/4-inch slices.
tips: Very large turnips or parsnips are often woody in the center — test by cutting through the middle before committing to a whole batch.
Parsnips become sweeter and more flavorful after cold storage or frost.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash, trim, and peel roots thoroughly. Cut into 1/2-inch cubes or slices. The USDA Complete Guide notes turnips and parsnips are processed similarly to carrots. Salt is optional: add 1/2 teaspoon per pint or 1 teaspoon per quart. Note: Turnips have a strong flavor that intensifies with canning — many people prefer to freeze rather than can turnips.
tips: Blanch cut pieces briefly in boiling water before packing to reduce strong flavors.
Consider freezing instead of canning for turnips — the texture and flavor hold up better when frozen.

sections.heading: Hot Pack
sections.body: Cover cut turnips or parsnips with boiling water and boil 5 minutes. Fill jars with hot pieces, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add salt if desired. Cover with hot cooking liquid, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles, wipe rims, adjust lids, and process.
tips: Discard the cooking water if you prefer a milder flavor — use fresh boiling water to fill jars.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Process in a pressure canner only — turnips and parsnips are low-acid vegetables. Water bath canning is not safe. Pints: 30 minutes. Quarts: 35 minutes. Weighted-gauge: 10 lb (0–1,000 ft), 15 lb (above 1,000 ft). Dial-gauge: 11 lb (0–2,000 ft).
tips: Processing times are the same as beets and similar to carrots.
Turnips and parsnips can be mixed in the same jar using these processing times.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Dial-gauge canners: 11 lb for 0–2,000 ft; 12 lb for 2,001–4,000 ft; 13 lb for 4,001–6,000 ft; 14 lb for 6,001–8,000 ft. Weighted-gauge canners: 10 lb for 0–1,000 ft; 15 lb above 1,000 ft.
tips: The same altitude pressure adjustments apply to all low-acid vegetable pressure canning.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 21 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 13-1/2 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 48 pounds and yields 14 to 19 quarts — an average of 2-3/4 pounds per quart.
tips: A food mill or ricer processes apples more quickly than peeling individually.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use any variety of apple that makes a good sauce. For best results, use a mixture of sweet and tart varieties.
tips: McIntosh, Cortland, and Golden Delicious are classic sauce apples.
Avoid using only a single super-sweet variety — the sauce can be cloying.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash, peel, and core apples. If desired, slice into water treated with ascorbic acid (3,000 mg per gallon) to prevent browning. Place drained apples in an 8- to 10-quart pot. Add 1/2 cup water. Stirring occasionally to prevent burning, heat quickly until tender (about 5 to 20 minutes, depending on maturity and variety). Press through a sieve or food mill, or skip the sieve for chunk-style. Add sugar to taste. Re-heat sauce to boiling; add 1/2 teaspoon cinnamon per quart, if desired. Fill jars with hot sauce, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Add sugar gradually and taste — ripe apples may need none.
Use minimal water to prevent a watery sauce.
Hot pack only; raw pack is not recommended for applesauce.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Peaches, Halved or Sliced
items.safety_notes: Treat cut surfaces with ascorbic acid solution to prevent browning.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 17-1/2 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 11 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 48 pounds and yields 16 to 24 quarts — an average of 2 to 3 pounds per quart.
tips: Purchase peaches in a flat or half-bushel for economy when canning large batches.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose ripe, mature fruit of ideal quality for eating fresh or cooking. Canning does not improve the quality of the fruit. Clingstone varieties are fine to use but freestone varieties are easier to pit and slice.
tips: Avoid peaches with green shoulders — they will not ripen further after picking.
Process in small batches to prevent browning.

sections.heading: Syrup
sections.body: The following syrups may be used. Extra-light: 1-1/4 cups sugar + 5-1/2 cups water = 6 cups syrup. Light: 2-1/4 cups sugar + 5-1/4 cups water = 6-1/2 cups syrup. Medium: 3-1/4 cups sugar + 5 cups water = 7 cups syrup. Heavy: 4-1/4 cups sugar + 4-1/4 cups water = 7 cups syrup. Very Heavy: 7 cups sugar + 3-3/4 cups water = 8-3/4 cups syrup. Dissolve sugar in water and heat to dissolve; skim foam. Light or extra-light syrup is recommended to preserve natural flavor. Water, apple juice, or white grape juice may be used instead of syrup.
tips: Extra-light or light syrup best preserves the natural peach flavor.
Use unsweetened fruit juice as a no-added-sugar alternative.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Dip fruit in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds until skins loosen. Dip quickly in cold water and slip off skins. Cut in half, remove pits, and slice if desired. To prevent browning, place prepared fruit in a solution of 3,000 mg ascorbic acid per gallon of water. Drain just before filling jars.
tips: Work in small batches and keep peeled fruit in ascorbic acid solution.
A melon baller removes the pit cavity cleanly after halving.

sections.heading: Procedure — Raw Pack
sections.body: Add 1/2 cup hot syrup, juice, or water to each hot quart jar. Fill jars with raw fruit, cavity side down and overlapping layers. Add hot syrup to cover fruit, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Heat drained fruit in syrup, water, or juice for 3 to 5 minutes. Fill hot jars with hot fruit and cooking liquid, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Hot pack results in a more uniform color and less floating fruit.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Pears, Halved
items.safety_notes: Asian pears are low-acid and must not be canned using these directions.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 17-1/2 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 11 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 50 pounds and yields 16 to 25 quarts — an average of 2-1/2 pounds per quart.
tips: Pick or buy pears while still firm; tree-ripe pears become mushy when canned.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose ripe, mature fruit of ideal quality. Bartlett (Williams) pears are the classic choice. Asian pears may be canned using the same method. Overripe pears will become very soft when processed.
tips: Pears should yield slightly to thumb pressure at the neck when ripe.
Avoid pears with a gritty texture throughout — they will remain gritty when canned.

sections.heading: Syrup
sections.body: Use extra-light, light, or medium syrup (see Peaches, Halved for syrup formulas). Light syrup is most commonly used for pears. Water or juice may substitute for syrup.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash and peel pears. Cut lengthwise in halves and remove cores. A melon baller or metal measuring spoon removes cores neatly. To prevent browning, immerse peeled fruit in a solution of 3,000 mg ascorbic acid per gallon of water.
tips: Remove the blossom end and the fibrous cord from core to stem.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack Only
sections.body: Heat pears in syrup, juice, or water for 5 minutes. Fill hot jars with hot fruit and cooking liquid, cavity side down, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Hot pack only is recommended for pears — raw pack is not tested.
Pack halves cavity-side down for the best use of jar space.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 19 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 12-1/4 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 48 pounds and yields 14 to 19 quarts of slices — an average of 2-3/4 pounds per quart.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select apples that are sweet, juicy, and crisp. For best results, use apple varieties that remain firm through processing such as Granny Smith, Rome Beauty, or Winesap. Avoid mealy or overripe fruit.
tips: Firm apple varieties hold their shape better after processing.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash, peel, and core apples. Slice into 1/2-inch wedges or rings. To prevent browning, place slices in water containing 3,000 mg ascorbic acid per gallon. Drain and rinse before heating.
tips: An apple slicer/corer tool speeds up preparation significantly.
Keep slices uniform in thickness for even heat penetration.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Place drained apple slices in a large saucepan and add 1 pint water or very light syrup per 5 pounds of apples. Boil 5 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent burning. Fill hot jars with apple slices and hot syrup or water, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 17-1/2 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 11 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 56 pounds and yields 22 to 32 quarts — an average of 2 pounds per quart.
tips: A cherry pitter makes pitting quick and keeps fruit intact.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select bright, uniformly colored, mature fruit of ideal quality for eating fresh or cooking. Both sweet and sour cherries may be canned. Sour cherries are preferred for pies and cobblers.
tips: Sour (tart) cherries have a higher natural acidity than sweet cherries.

sections.heading: Syrup
sections.body: For sweet cherries, use light or medium syrup. For sour cherries, use a medium to heavy syrup, or add sugar to taste. See Peaches section for full syrup formulas. Juice or water may be used in place of syrup.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash cherries. Remove stems and pits if desired — pitting is optional but unpitted cherries hold their shape better. If pitting, use a cherry/olive pitter. If canning unpitted, pierce skins to prevent splitting.
tips: Piercing unpitted cherries prevents blowout during processing.
Pitted cherries absorb syrup better but are softer after processing.

sections.heading: Procedure — Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with raw cherries, shaking down gently. Add hot syrup, juice, or water, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Combine cherries with syrup, juice, or water in a large saucepan. Bring to a boil. Fill hot jars with cherries and cooking liquid, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Hot pack reduces floating fruit significantly.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 14 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 9 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 56 pounds and yields 22 to 36 quarts — an average of 2 pounds per quart.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, ripe plums of good quality. Both freestone and clingstone varieties may be canned. Italian and Stanley prune-type plums hold their shape especially well.
tips: Prune plums (Italian) are firmer and less likely to fall apart when canned.

sections.heading: Syrup
sections.body: Light or medium syrup is recommended for sweet plums. See Peaches section for syrup formulas. Juice or water may substitute for syrup.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash plums. Freestone varieties may be halved and pitted. Clingstone varieties may be canned whole. Prick skins of whole plums on two sides to prevent splitting. To prevent browning of halved plums, place in ascorbic acid solution (3,000 mg per gallon of water).
tips: Prick whole plums with a needle or fork before processing.

sections.heading: Procedure — Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with raw plums, packing firmly. Add hot syrup, juice, or water, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Bring plums to a boil in syrup, juice, or water; boil 2 minutes. Cover and let stand 20 to 30 minutes. Fill hot jars with plums and cooking liquid, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: The stand time after boiling allows plums to absorb liquid and reduces floating.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Apricots, Halved or Sliced
items.safety_notes: Treat cut surfaces with ascorbic acid solution to prevent browning.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 16 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 10 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 50 pounds and yields 20 to 32 quarts — an average of 2 pounds per quart.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose ripe, mature fruit of ideal quality for eating fresh or cooking. Apricots should be uniformly colored (no green), firm, and free of blemishes. Overripe apricots will be very soft after processing.
tips: Apricots do not need peeling — skins are thin and palatable when canned.

sections.heading: Syrup
sections.body: Use extra-light or light syrup for best natural flavor. See Peaches section for syrup formulas. Juice or water may be used in place of syrup.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash fruit. Halve and pit; apricots do not require peeling. Slice if desired. To prevent browning, prepare in batches and place in a solution of 3,000 mg ascorbic acid per gallon of water until ready to fill jars.
tips: Apricot skins are thin enough to leave on — saves significant prep time.

sections.heading: Procedure — Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with raw apricot halves or slices, cavity side down. Add hot syrup, juice, or water, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Heat apricots in syrup, juice, or water for 3 to 5 minutes. Fill hot jars with fruit and cooking liquid, cavity side down, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Hot pack results in better color retention and less fruit floating.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Berries (Blackberries, Blueberries, Raspberries, Boysenberries)
items.safety_notes: Use firm, ripe berries. Strawberries are not recommended for this process — see Strawberry Jam.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 12 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 8 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. Berries typically yield 2 to 3 quarts per 6-pound flat, depending on berry size and how they are packed.
tips: Pick or purchase berries as close to canning day as possible — they deteriorate quickly.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose ripe, sweet berries with a uniform color. This procedure applies to blackberries, blueberries, raspberries, boysenberries, and similar soft fruits. Overripe or very soft berries will lose their shape in the jar.
tips: Sort and discard soft, moldy, or underripe berries before washing.

sections.heading: Syrup
sections.body: Use light or medium syrup, or use juice or water. See Peaches section for syrup formulas. Extra-light syrup best preserves the natural berry flavor and color.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash berries gently, a few at a time; drain. Remove stems and hulls. Blueberries: place in a single layer on a flat pan and freeze before packing (raw pack) — this allows them to be packed more tightly and still hold shape. Alternatively, heat 1/2 cup syrup per quart of berries to boiling, add berries, and boil 30 seconds (hot pack).
tips: Wash berries gently in a colander — do not soak.
Cold water rinse just before packing, not hours ahead.

sections.heading: Procedure — Raw Pack
