sections.body: Fill jars with raw berries, shaking down gently for a full pack. Cover with hot syrup, juice, or water, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Heat berries gently in syrup or juice for 30 seconds to 1 minute until heated through. Fill hot jars with berries and cooking liquid, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Hot pack greatly reduces floating with blueberries.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Figs
items.safety_notes: Figs are a low-acid fruit. Must add 2 tbsp bottled lemon juice or ¼ tsp citric acid per pint (double for quarts) directly to each jar before filling. Hot pack only.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 16 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 11 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A 36-pound lug yields 18 to 22 quarts.
tips: Figs must be picked fully ripe but still firm — overripe figs fall apart.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Figs do not need to be tree-ripe (fully soft) for canning; they should be fully colored but still firm. Do not can overripe, mushy figs.
tips: Brown Turkey and Calimyrna varieties can well; Kadota is also suitable.

sections.heading: Acid Addition — REQUIRED
sections.body: Figs are a low-acid food and MUST have acid added for safe water-bath canning. Add 2 tablespoons of bottled lemon juice per quart jar or 1 tablespoon per pint jar. Alternatively, add 1/2 teaspoon citric acid per quart or 1/4 teaspoon per pint.
tips: Never skip acid addition for figs — their pH can exceed 4.6.
Add acid to each jar before filling, not to the batch.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash figs gently in cold water. Do not peel or remove stems. Cover figs with water and boil 2 minutes; drain. Gently boil figs in light syrup for 5 minutes. Add 2 tablespoons bottled lemon juice per quart to each jar. Fill jars with hot figs and cooking syrup, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Handle figs gently to prevent bruising throughout preparation.
Use light syrup (2-1/4 cups sugar per 5-1/4 cups water) for figs.
Stems may be left on for appearance or trimmed close to the fruit.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Grape Juice
items.safety_notes: Strain juice to remove skins and seeds. Use the hot-fill method: heat juice to 190°F (do not boil), fill jars immediately.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 24-1/2 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts. A lug weighs 26 pounds and yields 7 to 9 quarts of juice.
tips: Concord grapes are the traditional choice for grape juice.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select sweet, well-colored, firm, mature fruit of ideal quality for eating fresh or cooking. The best flavor is obtained from a blend of slightly underripe and fully ripe grapes. Concord, Delaware, Catawba, and Niagara grapes are excellent choices.
tips: A small proportion of slightly underripe grapes improves the flavor balance.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash and stem grapes. Crush grapes and heat to boiling in a covered saucepan. Do not boil. Strain through a damp jelly bag or double layers of cheesecloth. Refrigerate juice for 24 to 48 hours. Without mixing, carefully pour off clear juice and discard sediment. Strain juice through a coffee filter or double cheesecloth. Add sugar to taste, if desired (1 to 2 tablespoons per quart is typical). Heat quickly to a boil. Fill hot quart or pint jars with hot juice, leaving 1/4-inch headspace. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Refrigerating juice for 24–48 hours allows tartrate crystals to settle out.
Do not shake or stir juice when pouring off the clear portion.
Straining through a coffee filter removes residual fine sediment.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Grapefruit and Orange Sections
items.safety_notes: Use only high-quality, ripe citrus. Remove all white pith. Sections can be packed in water, juice, or light syrup.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 15 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 13 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. Allow approximately 2-1/2 pounds of whole fruit per quart of sections.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, mature, high-quality fruit. Avoid over-mature or dry fruit. Navel oranges section easily; Valencia oranges are excellent for flavor. Ruby Red grapefruit holds color well after processing.
tips: Choose heavy fruit — heavier means juicier.
Thin-skinned fruit is easier to section.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash and peel fruit. Remove white pith from sections. Cut or tear sections free from membranes; work over a bowl to catch juice. Heat sections in syrup or juice. To remove bitterness from grapefruit, drop sections in boiling water for 1 minute; drain and proceed. Use very light or light syrup, or use unsweetened juice. Fill hot jars with hot fruit sections and syrup or juice, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Remove all pith to prevent a bitter flavor in the jar.
Blanching grapefruit sections in boiling water for 1 minute reduces bitterness.
Working over a bowl catches juice that can be used as packing liquid.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Nectarines, Halved or Sliced
items.safety_notes: Treat cut surfaces with ascorbic acid solution to prevent browning. Process times are the same as peaches.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 17-1/2 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 11 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. A bushel weighs 48 pounds and yields 16 to 24 quarts — an average of 2 to 3 pounds per quart.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose ripe, mature fruit of ideal quality for eating fresh or cooking. Nectarines are a fuzz-free peach variety and are canned using the same method. Avoid green-shouldered fruit.
tips: Nectarines do not require blanching to remove skins — skins are edible.
If peeling is desired, use the same boiling-water dip method as peaches.

sections.heading: Syrup
sections.body: Use extra-light, light, or medium syrup. See Peaches section for syrup formulas. Juice or water may be used in place of syrup.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash nectarines. Peeling is optional: dip in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds to loosen skins if desired, then cool and slip off skins. Halve and pit; slice if desired. To prevent browning, place prepared fruit in a solution of 3,000 mg ascorbic acid per gallon of water.
tips: Nectarines can be canned unpeeled — skin softens during processing.

sections.heading: Procedure — Raw Pack
sections.body: Fill jars with raw fruit, cavity side down. Add hot syrup, juice, or water, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Heat drained fruit in syrup, juice, or water for 3 to 5 minutes. Fill hot jars with hot fruit and cooking liquid, cavity side down, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Pineapple
items.safety_notes: Use only fully ripe pineapple. Unripe pineapple is unsafe. Hot pack only.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 21 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 13 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. Whole pineapples average 2 to 5 pounds each; yield approximately 50 percent edible fruit after peeling, coring, and trimming.
tips: A dedicated pineapple corer-slicer tool speeds preparation significantly.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, ripe pineapples with a fragrant aroma at the stem end. Overripe pineapple will be very soft and break apart during processing. Underripe pineapple will be starchy and flavorless.
tips: A ripe pineapple smells sweet at the base and has golden-yellow skin.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash pineapple. Cut off top and base. Peel deeply enough to remove all eyes. Quarter lengthwise and remove core. Slice, cube, or cut into chunks. If desired, use a pineapple corer for uniform rings.
tips: Remove the tough center core — it remains fibrous even after canning.

sections.heading: Procedure — Hot Pack
sections.body: Heat pineapple in syrup, juice, or water: bring to boil and cook for 10 minutes. Pack hot pineapple into hot jars and cover with hot cooking liquid or juice, leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Unsweetened pineapple juice is an ideal packing liquid for this fruit.
Hot pack only is recommended for pineapple — raw pack is not tested.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Rhubarb
items.safety_notes: Rhubarb leaves are toxic — use stalks only. Hot pack only. Often sweetened before packing.

sections.heading: Quantity
sections.body: An average of 10-1/2 pounds is needed per canner load of 7 quarts; an average of 7 pounds per canner load of 9 pints. Allow 1-1/2 to 2 pounds of rhubarb per quart.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select young, tender, well-colored stalks with few strings. Stalks should be at least 1 inch in diameter and no longer than about 18 inches. Discard leaves — they are poisonous. Never eat rhubarb leaves.
tips: NEVER consume rhubarb leaves — they contain oxalic acid and are toxic.
Young, red-pink stalks have the best flavor and color when canned.

sections.heading: Preparation & Procedure
sections.body: Wash and trim stalks. Discard leaves. Cut into 1/2- to 1-inch pieces. In a large bowl, combine rhubarb and 1/2 cup sugar per quart of rhubarb. Let stand 3 to 4 hours to draw out juice. Bring slowly to a boil, stirring gently. Fill hot pint or quart jars with hot rhubarb and syrup (the juice drawn from the rhubarb), leaving 1/2-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Adjust lids and process.
tips: The 3–4 hour draw-out step is important — do not skip it.
Add more sugar to taste if the rhubarb is very tart.
Rhubarb softens significantly during processing — expect a soft, saucy pack.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Water Bath Canner — increase processing time: 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 min; 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 min; 6,001–8,000 ft add 15 min; 8,001–10,000 ft add 20 min.

items.name: Jams and Soft Spreads (General)
items.safety_notes: Use only tested recipes.

sections.heading: General Principles
sections.body:
The following types of jellied products are described in this guide: Jelly is made from fruit juice; the product is clear and firm enough to hold its shape when turned out of the container. Jam is made from crushed or chopped fruits and sugar; jam does not gel as firmly as jelly. Preserves are made of small whole fruits or uniform-size pieces of fruit in a clear, thick, slightly gelled syrup. Conserves are jam-like products made from a mixture of fruits, usually including citrus. Marmalade is a soft fruit jelly with small pieces of fruit or peel evenly suspended in a transparent jelly. Fruit butters are made from fruit pulp cooked with sugar to a thick, spreadable consistency.

The standard ingredients for making jellied fruit products are fruit, pectin, acid, and sugar. The proportions of these four ingredients affect the flavor of the product as well as whether or not the product will gel. A proper gel depends on the correct balance of all four ingredients.
tips: Pectin, acid, and sugar must all be in correct proportion to gel.
Follow tested recipes exactly — do not reduce sugar.
Use ripe, undamaged fruit for best flavor and natural pectin.

sections.heading: Pectin
sections.body: Pectin is a natural substance found in ripe fruits. Fruits that are naturally high in pectin include: sour (tart) apples, crab apples, sour blackberries, boysenberries, gooseberries, concord grapes, plums, quinces, currants, and some varieties of loganberries. Fruits that are naturally low in pectin include: blueberries, cherries, figs, peaches, pears, pomegranates, raspberries, strawberries, and sweet apples. Commercial pectin products are available in liquid and powder forms, and are made from apples or citrus peel. Pectin should be used by the expiration date. If using commercial pectin, follow the manufacturer's directions exactly — do not interchange liquid and powder pectin.
tips: Do not interchange liquid and powdered pectin in recipes.
Check expiration date on commercial pectin before using.
Slightly under-ripe fruit blended with ripe fruit boosts natural pectin.

sections.heading: Gel Testing
sections.body: There are three ways to test for a proper gel when not using commercial pectin. Temperature test: Use a jelly or candy thermometer and boil until mixture reaches 220°F (8°F above the boiling point of water at sea level). At 1,000 ft, boil to 218°F; at 2,000 ft, boil to 216°F; at 3,000 ft, boil to 214°F. Spoon or sheet test: Dip a cool metal spoon into the boiling jelly mixture. Raise the spoon out of the steam, about 12 inches above the kettle. Turn the spoon so the liquid runs off the side. The jelly is done when two drops of liquid form along the edge of the spoon and flow together and sheet off the spoon. Refrigerator/freezer test: Pour a small amount of boiling jelly on a cold plate and put it in the freezing compartment of a refrigerator for a few minutes. If the mixture gels, it is ready.
tips: Temperature test is most reliable — thermometer reads 220°F at sea level.
Sheet test: two drops merge and sheet off the spoon.
Refrigerator test: a dollop on a cold plate should gel in 2 minutes.
Subtract 2°F per 1,000 ft elevation for temperature test.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Use half-pint or pint canning jars. Sterilize jars if the water bath process is under 10 minutes. Use new lids each time. All jams and soft spreads should be processed in a boiling water bath canner. Fill hot jars with hot jam, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Adjust lids. Process 5 to 10 minutes depending on jar size and recipe. After processing, allow jars to cool 12 to 24 hours before checking seals.
tips: Sterilize jars if processing less than 10 minutes.
Leave ¼-inch headspace for jams and jellies.
Allow 24 hours for full gel to set after processing.
Do not tilt or move jars until fully cooled and gelled.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Increase processing time if you live at altitudes above 1,000 feet. At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes to base processing time.

sections.heading: General Principles
sections.body: Jelly is made from the juice of the fruit. The best jellies are firm enough to hold their shape when turned out of the jar, yet quiver when moved. They are tender and cut easily with a spoon. They are clear and sparkling with a fresh fruit flavor. Use only fully ripe fruit for extracting juice — overripe fruit is lower in pectin. Mix ¼ underripe fruit with ¾ fully ripe fruit to boost natural pectin.
tips: Use ¼ slightly under-ripe + ¾ ripe fruit for natural pectin boost.
Never squeeze the juice bag — squeezing causes cloudy jelly.
Strain juice through damp cheesecloth or a jelly bag.

sections.heading: Juice Extraction
sections.body: Wash all fruits thoroughly before cooking. Remove stems, skins, and pits as directed in specific recipes. Cut fruits into small pieces. Crush soft fruits. Add water as directed. Bring fruit and water to a boil; reduce heat and simmer until fruit is soft. Pour prepared fruit into a damp jelly bag or double layer of cheesecloth in a colander set in a bowl. Let drip — do not squeeze the bag or the jelly will be cloudy.
tips: Let juice drip overnight for the clearest jelly.
Never squeeze the jelly bag.
Discard or compost the spent fruit pulp.

sections.heading: Gel Testing
sections.body: When making jelly without added pectin, test for gel by: Temperature test — boil to 220°F (8°F above boiling point of water at sea level). Sheet test — dip a metal spoon into the boiling liquid; if two drops slide together and sheet off the edge, it is done. Freezer test — place a small amount on a cold plate; return to freezer for 2 minutes; if it gels, the jelly is ready.
tips: 220°F at sea level is the target endpoint temperature.
Use a reliable candy thermometer; verify its accuracy in boiling water.
Sheet test: two drops must merge and sheet off, not drip individually.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Measure juice into a large saucepot. If using commercial pectin, follow manufacturer's directions. If not, add sugar according to recipe (usually ¾ cup sugar per cup of juice). Bring to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Boil to gel point. Remove from heat; skim foam. Fill sterilized half-pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Wipe rims. Adjust lids. Process 5 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Skim foam immediately before filling jars.
Fill jars quickly — jelly begins to set as it cools.
Process 5 minutes (half-pints) in boiling water bath.
Sterilize jars when processing 10 minutes or less.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Adjust gel-point temperature: subtract 2°F per 1,000 ft elevation. Increase water bath processing time: at 1,001–3,000 ft add 5 minutes; at 3,001–6,000 ft add 10 minutes; above 6,000 ft add 15 minutes.
tips: At 5,000 ft, target gel temperature is 210°F instead of 220°F.

items.name: Apple Butter
items.safety_notes: Use only a tested recipe. Cook until thick — a spoonful placed on a chilled plate should not weep liquid around the edges.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use any variety of ripe, quality apple. A mixture of apple varieties gives a more complex flavor. Avoid using overripe, moldy, or damaged apples. Remove all damaged portions. Tart apples give apple butter a better flavor and natural acidity.
tips: Blend tart and sweet apple varieties for best flavor.
Use culled apples if unblemished — cut out all bad spots.
Windfall apples are fine if freshly fallen and undamaged.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash apples. Remove stems and blossom ends; do not peel or core. Cut into pieces. Barely cover with water; cook until soft. Press through a food mill or sieve. Measure pulp. For each cup of pulp, add ½ cup sugar (or to taste). Add cinnamon, cloves, and other spices as desired.
tips: Cooking unpeeled apples gives richer color and flavor.
A food mill removes skins and seeds automatically.
Taste pulp and adjust sugar before long cooking begins.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Cook pulp and sugar mixture slowly, stirring frequently to prevent sticking, until thick enough to round up on a spoon — no liquid should separate around edges. Add spices during the last 30 minutes of cooking. Fill hot pint or half-pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process half-pints and pints 5 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Stir constantly near end — apple butter scorches easily.
Done test: a spoonful on a plate should hold its shape.
Add spices near end to preserve volatile flavor compounds.
Half-pints and pints: 5 minutes.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 8 half-pints from 8 pounds of apples.
tips: Apple butter keeps best in the refrigerator after opening.

items.name: Apple Jelly
items.safety_notes: Use a jelly bag or fine cloth to strain juice. Do not squeeze bag or jelly will be cloudy.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use tart, firm apples for the most pectin and best gel. Crab apples are excellent. Mix ¼ underripe with ¾ ripe for highest pectin. Do not use overripe apples — pectin decreases as fruit ripens beyond peak.
tips: Tart apple varieties (Granny Smith, crab apple) have the most pectin.
Mix slightly under-ripe and ripe for best gel.
Do not use mealy or overripe apples.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Sort, wash, and remove stem and blossom ends from apples. Do not peel or core. Cut apples into small chunks. Add 1 cup water per pound of fruit. Bring to a boil; reduce heat and simmer until apples are soft, about 20 to 25 minutes. Strain through a damp jelly bag or cheesecloth. Let drip undisturbed — do not squeeze.
tips: Cook with skins and seeds — they add pectin.
Let juice drip at least 2 hours, or overnight for clarity.
Measure juice accurately before proceeding.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Measure apple juice into a large saucepot. For each cup of juice, add ¾ cup sugar. Stir to dissolve. Bring to a full rolling boil over high heat, stirring constantly. Boil hard until gel point (220°F at sea level). Remove from heat; skim foam. Fill sterilized half-pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Wipe rims. Process 5 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: A full rolling boil cannot be stirred down — watch the pot.
Skim foam for the clearest jelly.
Half-pints: 5 minutes in boiling water bath.
Gel forms as jelly cools — allow 24 hours before judging set.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Adjust gel-point temperature by subtracting 2°F per 1,000 ft. Increase water bath process time: add 5 min at 1,001–3,000 ft; add 10 min at 3,001–6,000 ft; add 15 min above 6,000 ft.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 5 to 6 half-pints from 3 pounds of apples.

items.name: Grape Jelly
items.safety_notes: Let juice stand in refrigerator overnight to allow tartrate crystals to settle; strain before using.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Concord and other slip-skin grapes are traditional for jelly. Use fully ripe grapes for best flavor; include a few slightly underripe grapes for extra pectin. Remove grapes from stems; discard overripe, soft, or moldy fruit.
tips: Concord grapes give classic grape jelly flavor.
Include 10–15% slightly underripe grapes for natural pectin.
Remove all stems before cooking.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash grapes and remove stems. Crush grapes thoroughly in a large saucepot. For Concord grapes, add ½ cup water per pound. Bring to a boil; simmer 10 minutes. Strain juice through a damp jelly bag; let drip undisturbed. Refrigerate juice overnight to allow tartrate crystals to settle. Do not squeeze the bag. Strain again through two layers of damp cheesecloth before using.
tips: Refrigerate juice overnight and strain again to prevent crystal formation in jars.
Never squeeze the jelly bag — cloudiness results.
Concord grapes: add ½ cup water per pound; other grapes may need less.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Measure juice into a large pot. Add ¾ cup sugar per cup of juice (or follow a tested recipe). Bring to a rolling boil, stirring to dissolve sugar. Boil hard to gel point (220°F at sea level). Remove from heat; skim foam. Fill sterilized half-pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Wipe rims. Process 5 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Skim foam for clear jelly.
Half-pints: 5 minutes in boiling water bath.
Do not move jars for 12–24 hours after processing.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Subtract 2°F from gel temperature per 1,000 ft elevation. Add 5 min process time at 1,001–3,000 ft; 10 min at 3,001–6,000 ft; 15 min above 6,000 ft.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 8 half-pints from 3½ pounds of grapes.

items.name: Strawberry Jam
items.safety_notes: Use fully ripe strawberries. Do not reduce sugar — sugar is required for proper gel and safety.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select fully ripe, firm, deep-red strawberries. Avoid overripe, soft, or moldy berries. Smaller berries tend to have more flavor than large commercial varieties. Process within 2 days of picking for best color and flavor.
tips: Small, fragrant berries make the best jam.
Use within 2 days of harvest; refrigerate until ready.
Discard any moldy or mushy berries — mold can ruin a whole batch.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Sort and wash berries. Remove caps and stems. Crush berries one layer at a time using a potato masher. For a smoother jam, crush more thoroughly; for a chunkier jam, leave some pieces. Measure crushed berries. Strawberries are naturally low in pectin, so commercial pectin (liquid or powdered) is commonly used.
tips: Crush berries in layers for uniform texture.
Measure crushed fruit accurately — recipe ratios are critical.
Do not use a blender — it incorporates too much air.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: With added pectin (typical method): combine crushed strawberries and pectin in a large saucepot. Bring to a full rolling boil over high heat, stirring constantly. Add sugar all at once. Return to a full rolling boil; boil hard 1 minute, stirring constantly. Remove from heat; skim foam. Fill hot half-pint or pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Wipe rims. Process half-pints and pints 10 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Add all sugar at once after the first boil when using pectin.
Boil exactly 1 minute after adding sugar — no longer.
Skim foam before ladling into jars.
Half-pints and pints: 10 minutes.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 8 half-pints from 2 quarts of crushed strawberries with added pectin.
tips: Jam may appear loose when hot — it firms as it cools.

items.name: Peach Jam
items.safety_notes: Use ripe, firm peaches. Add 2 tbsp lemon juice per batch to brighten flavor and improve gel.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select ripe, mature, high-quality peaches. Soft, overripe peaches may be used if they have no mold or rot. Freestone varieties are easier to pit. Peaches are low in natural pectin, so commercial pectin is recommended for a reliable set.
tips: Ripe but firm peaches give best texture.
Freestone varieties are much easier to work with than clingstone.
Peel, pit, and crush peaches immediately before cooking.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash peaches. To peel: dip in boiling water 30 to 60 seconds, then in cold water; skins slip off. Remove pits. Crush peaches using a potato masher. To prevent browning, add 1 teaspoon ascorbic acid or ¼ teaspoon powdered vitamin C per quart of crushed peaches. Measure crushed fruit.
tips: Blanch-peel in boiling water for easy skin removal.
Add ascorbic acid to prevent browning of crushed fruit.
Work quickly — peaches discolor rapidly when cut.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: With added pectin: combine measured crushed peaches and pectin in a large saucepot. Add 2 tablespoons lemon juice per batch for additional acidity. Bring to a full rolling boil, stirring constantly. Add measured sugar all at once. Return to rolling boil; boil hard 1 minute, stirring constantly. Remove from heat; skim foam. Fill hot half-pint or pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Wipe rims. Process half-pints 10 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Add lemon juice for extra acid and better gel.
Boil exactly 1 minute with sugar — overcooking darkens jam.
Half-pints and pints: 10 minutes.
Skim off foam before filling jars.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 5 to 6 half-pints from 3 pounds of peaches.
tips: Peach jam darkens slightly over time — this is normal.

items.name: Berry Jam (Blackberry, Raspberry, Blueberry)
items.safety_notes: Use fully ripe berries. Do not reduce sugar.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use fully ripe blackberries, raspberries, or blueberries. Blackberries and raspberries have more natural pectin than blueberries; commercial pectin is recommended for all three for a reliable set. Avoid moldy or overripe berries that have begun to ferment.
tips: Process berries the same day as harvesting for best color.
Remove any leaves, stems, or underripe berries.
Crush just before cooking — crushed berries deteriorate quickly.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Sort and wash berries gently. Drain. Crush berries one layer at a time. For seedless blackberry or raspberry jam, press crushed berries through a food mill or fine sieve to remove seeds. Measure crushed or sieved pulp. Follow a tested recipe for berry type.
tips: Crush gently to avoid over-processing.
Sieve for seedless jam — seeds become tough after processing.
Measure accurately: too much fruit makes runny jam.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: With added pectin: combine crushed berries and pectin in a large saucepot. Bring to a full rolling boil, stirring constantly. Add measured sugar (usually 4–5 cups) all at once. Return to a full rolling boil; boil hard exactly 1 minute, stirring constantly. Remove from heat; skim foam. Fill hot half-pint or pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Wipe rims. Process 10 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Full rolling boil: can't be stirred down — then add sugar.
Boil exactly 1 minute after sugar addition.
Half-pints and pints: 10 minutes.
Skim foam immediately before filling.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 7 to 8 half-pints from 2 quarts of crushed berries with added commercial pectin.
tips: Raspberry jam seeds are preferred by some; sieve if not.

items.name: Orange Marmalade
items.safety_notes: Use only tested recipe. Do not alter sugar or citrus proportions. Marmalade requires proper gel set — test with cold plate method.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use thin-skinned, ripe oranges. Seville (bitter) oranges are traditional for marmalade. Sweet navel or Valencia oranges may be used. Lemons are added for extra pectin and acid. Avoid fruit with thick, pithy rinds — the pith becomes bitter.
tips: Thin-skinned oranges have less bitter pith.
Add 1–2 lemons per batch for extra pectin and brightness.
Organic or unsprayed fruit is best since peel is used.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash fruit well. Remove peel in thin strips using a vegetable peeler or zester; remove as much white pith from peel as possible. Cut peel into thin shreds. Remove white pith from fruit; section or chop pulp, reserving juice. Tie seeds and membrane in cheesecloth bag. Combine peel, pulp, juice, cheesecloth bag, and water. Soak overnight or simmer until peel is tender. Remove cheesecloth bag.
tips: Remove as much white pith from peel as possible — it is very bitter.
Thin-cut peel gives more elegant marmalade than thick chunks.
Soaking overnight softens peel and extracts natural pectin from seeds.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Measure fruit mixture. For each cup, add ¾ to 1 cup sugar (follow tested recipe). Bring mixture to a rolling boil over high heat, stirring to dissolve sugar. Boil hard to gel point (220°F at sea level), stirring frequently. Remove from heat; skim foam. Stir and skim for 5 minutes to cool slightly and distribute peel. Fill hot sterilized half-pint jars, leaving ¼-inch headspace. Wipe rims. Process 10 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Stir 5 minutes off heat before jarring — prevents peel floating to top.
Sterilize jars before filling for best results.
Half-pints: 10 minutes in boiling water bath.
220°F is the gel point at sea level.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Subtract 2°F from gel temperature per 1,000 ft elevation. Add 5 min process time at 1,001–3,000 ft; 10 min at 3,001–6,000 ft; 15 min above 6,000 ft.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 7 to 8 half-pints from 6 medium oranges and 2 lemons.
tips: Allow 2 weeks before opening — marmalade flavor mellows over time.
Refrigerate after opening.

items.name: Dill Pickles
items.safety_notes: Use 4–6% acidity vinegar. Do not reduce vinegar or increase water. Use pickling/canning salt only.
items.altitude_note: +5 min for 1,001–6,000 ft · +10 min above 6,000 ft

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only unwaxed, pickling cucumbers. 'Slicing' cucumbers will give you a soft pickle. Measure or weigh amounts carefully, because the proportion of fresh vegetables to other ingredients will affect the flavor and, in many instances, the safety of the pickled product. Use cucumbers 1½ to 4 inches in length for whole dills. For soft pickles, discard a thin slice from the blossom end.
tips: Use unwaxed pickling cucumbers only — slicers make soft pickles.
Remove ¼-inch slice from blossom end to prevent softening.
Use cucumbers within 24 hours of harvest for crispest pickles.
Discard any cucumbers that are soft, shriveled, or diseased.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash cucumbers well, especially around the stem area. Do not use cucumbers that have soft spots or damaged areas. For quick fresh-pack dill pickles: wash cucumbers; slice ¼ inch off blossom end. Cover cucumbers with boiling water; let stand 30 minutes. Combine vinegar, water, and salt in a large pot and bring to a boil.
tips: Scrub cucumbers gently with a soft vegetable brush.
Soak in ice water 2 hours before packing for extra crispness.
Use 5% acidity vinegar — do not dilute below tested ratios.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Place ½ teaspoon of dill seed or 1 head of fresh dill weed per pint in the bottom of each sterile pint jar. Add cucumbers, one clove of garlic, and 2 sprigs of fresh dill per jar. Combine 3 cups vinegar, 3 cups water, and 3 tablespoons canning salt; bring to a boil. Pour boiling pickling solution over cucumbers, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe jar rims. Process in boiling water bath canner: pints 10 minutes, quarts 15 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Leave ½-inch headspace for all pickle products.
Use canning/pickling salt — table salt causes cloudy brine.
Process in boiling water bath immediately after filling.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Increase processing time if you live at altitudes above 1,000 feet. At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.
tips: Always add extra time for altitude in water bath canning.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 7 to 9 pints. An average of 14 pounds of cucumbers (3- to 4-inch pickling) is needed per 7-quart canner load.
tips: Allow 4–5 weeks before tasting for flavors to develop.

items.name: Bread and Butter Pickles
items.safety_notes: Use 4–6% acidity vinegar. Use pickling/canning salt only.
items.altitude_note: +5 min for 1,001–6,000 ft · +10 min above 6,000 ft

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only unwaxed pickling cucumbers. Select firm, fresh cucumbers 1½ to 4 inches in length. Remove ¼ inch from blossom end. The blossom end contains enzymes that can soften pickles.
tips: Use fresh, firm cucumbers — never soft or yellowed ones.
Remove blossom-end slice to prevent enzyme softening.
Sweet onions give the best flavor.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash and drain cucumbers. Remove ¼ inch from blossom end. Slice cucumbers and onions ¼-inch thick. For each quart of sliced cucumbers and onions, add ¼ cup of canning salt. Cover with 2 inches of crushed or cubed ice. Refrigerate 3 to 4 hours. Add more ice as needed. Drain well.
tips: Ice-brine soak is essential — do not skip or shorten.
Drain and rinse slices thoroughly after salting.
Uniform ¼-inch slices process more evenly.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Combine vinegar, sugar, and spices in a large pot. Add drained cucumber-onion slices and heat to a boil. Fill hot pint or quart jars with hot pickle mixture, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints 10 minutes, quarts 15 minutes in a boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Leave ½-inch headspace.
Use distilled white or apple-cider vinegar at 5% acidity.
Do not reduce sugar or vinegar — affects safety and gel.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes to base time.
tips: Always apply altitude adjustment for water bath canning.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 8 pints. An average of 6 pounds of cucumbers is needed per 8 pints.
tips: Wait 2 weeks before opening to allow flavors to develop.

items.name: Pickled Beets
items.safety_notes: Use 5% acidity vinegar. Do not reduce vinegar or increase water.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select 1½- to 2-inch diameter beets for best results. Beets larger than 3 inches may be tough or fibrous. Remove beet tops but leave 1 inch of the stem and the taproot to prevent bleeding of color.
tips: Small, uniform beets give the best texture.
Leave 1-inch stem and taproot to retain color during cooking.
Avoid beets with white rings — they lack good flavor.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash and sort beets by size. Cook similar-size beets together. Boil until skins slip off easily (25 to 30 minutes for small beets). Cool and remove skins, stems, and taproots. Leave baby beets whole. Cut medium or large beets into ½-inch slices. Quarter large slices.
tips: Cook beets before peeling — do not peel raw.
Cool in cold water briefly before peeling.
Slice uniformly for even vinegar penetration.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Combine 2 cups vinegar (5% acidity), 1½ cups sugar, 1 cup water, and 2 teaspoons canning salt in a saucepan; bring to a boil. Pack beets into hot pint or quart jars, leaving ½-inch headspace. Add hot pickling solution, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints and quarts 30 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Pints and quarts both process 30 minutes.
Do not reduce vinegar-to-sugar ratio.
Pack beets firmly but do not crush.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.
tips: Altitude adjustment applies to the full 30-minute base time.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 3 pounds of beets without tops per quart. About 7 quarts per canner load of average beets.
tips: Color from beets may stain — protect work surfaces.

items.name: Pickled Asparagus
items.safety_notes: Use 5% acidity white or cider vinegar. Use only firm, fresh spears. Do not alter vinegar proportions.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select young, tender, tight-tipped asparagus spears. Use spears 4 to 4½ inches long to fit pint jars. For quarts, use spears up to 6¼ inches. Process within 2 hours of harvest for best quality.
tips: Use freshly harvested, firm asparagus with tight tips.
Cut spears to uniform height for the jar size used.
Process the same day as harvest for crispest pickles.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash asparagus spears thoroughly. Trim woody ends. Wash again. For pints, cut spears to 4 to 4½ inches. For quarts, cut to 6 to 6¼ inches. Prepare brine: combine vinegar, water, canning salt, and sugar if desired. Bring to a boil.
tips: Trim and cut spears to consistent length before packing.
Use distilled white vinegar for brightest green color.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Pack asparagus tightly into hot pint or quart jars, tips up or down (tips up preferred). Add garlic and hot peppers if desired. Pour boiling brine over asparagus, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints 10 minutes, quarts 10 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Pack spears tightly — they shrink during processing.
Leave ½-inch headspace.
Pints and quarts: same 10-minute process time.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 2½ pounds of asparagus per quart. About 7 quarts per canner load.

items.name: Pickled Dilled Carrots
items.safety_notes: Use 5% acidity vinegar. Do not alter vinegar or water proportions.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, crisp, fresh carrots. Use carrots 1 to 1¼ inches in diameter for sticks or coins. Avoid large, pithy carrots. Fresh-harvested carrots give the best texture.
tips: Choose slender, firm carrots — avoid large woody ones.
Peel carrots for best flavor absorption.
Process same day as purchase or harvest.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash and peel carrots. Cut into strips or ¼-inch coins. Prepare brine with vinegar, water, salt, and dill. Bring brine to a boil. Pack raw carrots tightly into hot pint jars.
tips: Cut uniform sticks or rounds for even processing.
Fresh dill weed or dill seed both work well.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Pack carrot sticks or coins tightly into hot pint jars. Add 1 head fresh dill or 1 teaspoon dill seed per jar. Pour boiling brine (1½ cups vinegar, 1½ cups water, 2 tablespoons canning salt) over carrots, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints 15 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Pints only: 15 minutes.
Pack carrots tightly — they will shrink slightly.
Use 5% acidity vinegar only.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 9 pints from 3 pounds of carrots.

items.name: Pickled Sweet Peppers
items.safety_notes: Use 5% acidity vinegar. Do not alter vinegar proportions. Wash hands after handling peppers.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, fresh sweet peppers free of soft spots, wrinkles, or blemishes. Use any color: green, red, yellow, or orange. Hungarian wax peppers may also be used. Use within 2 days of harvest.
tips: Use firm, crisp peppers — discard any with soft spots.
Mix colors for a visually appealing product.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash peppers well. Remove stems, seeds, and cores. Quarter peppers or leave as halves. Blanch peppers in boiling water or blister skins under a broiler and peel. Flatten small peppers.
tips: Roasting or blistering gives better flavor and easier peeling.
Remove all seeds and membranes.
Wear gloves even with sweet peppers if handling large quantities.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Combine 5 cups vinegar, 1 cup water, 2 teaspoons canning salt, and ¼ cup sugar; bring to a boil. Flatten small peppers; halve or quarter large ones. Fill hot pint jars with peppers. Pour boiling brine over peppers, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints and half-pints 10 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Pints and half-pints: 10 minutes.
Add 1 clove garlic per jar if desired.
Do not use quart jars for pickled peppers.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 9 half-pints. An average of 9 pounds of peppers per 9 half-pint jars.

items.name: Pickled Hot Peppers
items.safety_notes: Use 5% acidity vinegar. Wear rubber or plastic gloves when handling hot peppers — do not touch eyes or face. Do not alter vinegar proportions.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select firm, fresh hot peppers. Jalapeño, cayenne, serrano, and Hungarian wax peppers are all suitable. Use within 2 days of harvest for best quality. Small peppers may be canned whole; larger ones may be quartered.
tips: Wear rubber or latex gloves when handling hot peppers — capsaicin burns.
Do not touch face or eyes while working with hot peppers.
Discard any soft, moldy, or blemished peppers.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash peppers well. If small, leave whole with two small slits in each. Quarter large peppers and remove seeds and membranes. Blanch in boiling water or blister and peel skin if desired. Prepare brine with vinegar, water, and salt.
tips: Slash whole peppers to allow brine penetration.
Removing seeds reduces heat level.
Skin may be left on small whole peppers.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Fill hot pint or half-pint jars with peppers. Add 1 clove garlic per jar if desired. Combine 5 cups vinegar and 1 cup water; bring to a boil. Pour brine over peppers, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints and half-pints 10 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Half-pints and pints: 10 minutes.
Do not pack peppers too tightly — brine must circulate.
Use 5% acidity vinegar; do not dilute.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 9 half-pints. An average of 9 pounds of peppers per 9 half-pint jars.

items.name: Pickled Green Tomatoes, Dilled
items.safety_notes: Use 5% acidity vinegar. Use only firm, fully green tomatoes. Do not alter vinegar proportions.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use hard, green tomatoes with no color showing. Do not use tomatoes that have begun to ripen. Select tomatoes of uniform size for consistent texture. Remove stem scars.
tips: Use fully green, unripe tomatoes only.
Small to medium tomatoes work best — large ones may be pithy.
Remove all stem scars and wash thoroughly.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash green tomatoes. Remove stem scars. Cut out any blemishes. Leave small tomatoes whole; halve or quarter large ones. Prepare dill brine: combine vinegar, water, and canning salt; bring to a boil. Add fresh dill or dill seed to jars.
tips: Slice into ¼-inch rounds for more even pickling.
Add garlic and peppercorns for extra flavor.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Add 1 to 2 heads fresh dill or 1 to 2 teaspoons dill seed to each pint jar. Pack tomatoes into hot pint jars. Pour boiling brine (1 cup vinegar, 1 cup water, 1 tablespoon canning salt) over tomatoes, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints 15 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Pints: 15 minutes in boiling water bath.
Leave ½-inch headspace.
Do not use quart jars for this product.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 9 pints from approximately 10 to 11 pounds of green tomatoes.
tips: Allow at least 2 weeks before opening to develop full flavor.

items.name: Corn Relish
items.safety_notes: Use only a USDA-tested recipe. Do not change proportions of vegetables, vinegar, or sugar. Use 5% acidity vinegar.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Select ears of corn with bright green husks, fresh silks, and plump but not fully mature kernels. Kernels at the milk stage give the best color and texture. Avoid starchy, over-mature corn.
tips: Use fresh corn at the milk stage — press a kernel; it should squirt milky juice.
Process within 2 hours of harvest for best color.
Frozen corn kernels may be substituted off-season.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Husk and clean corn. Cook in boiling water 5 minutes. Dip in cold water. Cut kernels from cob — do not scrape. Measure 10 cups of corn kernels. Combine with chopped sweet and hot peppers, celery, onion, and a vinegar-sugar-spice brine.
tips: Cut kernels off; do not scrape — scraped corn goes mushy.
Cool ears in ice water before cutting for cleaner kernels.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Combine all vegetables with 2½ cups vinegar, ¾ cup sugar, 2 teaspoons canning salt, and spices in a large pot. Bring to boil; simmer 20 minutes. Fill hot pint jars with hot relish mixture, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints 15 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Pints: 15 minutes.
Stir relish frequently during the 20-minute simmer.
Do not reduce sugar or vinegar ratios.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 9 pints. Approximately 18 to 20 ears of corn yield 10 cups of kernels.

items.name: Piccalilli
items.safety_notes: Use 5% acidity vinegar. Use only a tested recipe — do not alter vegetable or vinegar proportions.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use firm, fresh vegetables. Green tomatoes, cabbage, sweet peppers, onions, and cucumbers are traditional. All vegetables must be at their prime — no over-ripe or spoiled vegetables should be used.
tips: Use a mix of fresh, firm vegetables for best texture.
Uniform chopping gives even texture in the finished relish.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Chop all vegetables finely or coarsely as preferred. Combine all chopped vegetables with ¼ cup canning salt; let stand 4 to 8 hours. Drain and rinse well in cold water. Squeeze out as much liquid as possible. Prepare vinegar-sugar-spice brine.
tips: Salt-and-drain step draws out moisture for crunchier relish.
Rinse thoroughly after draining to remove excess salt.
Squeeze vegetables in cheesecloth for driest result.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Combine drained vegetables with vinegar, sugar, and spices. Bring to a boil; simmer 30 minutes until slightly thickened. Fill hot pint jars with hot mixture, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints 10 minutes in boiling water bath (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Pints: 10 minutes.
Stir frequently during the simmer to prevent scorching.
Relish thickens slightly as it cools.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 9 half-pints from approximately 6 pounds of mixed vegetables.
tips: Flavor improves after 2 weeks; best after 4 weeks.

items.name: Watermelon Pickles
items.safety_notes: Use only the white rind portion — remove all pink flesh and green skin. Use 5% acidity vinegar.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use the thick white rind of mature watermelons. The rind should be firm and white, not pink or green. Remove all green skin and pink flesh before using. Immature melons will have thin rinds with little usable material.
tips: Choose large, mature watermelons for the thickest rind.
Trim all green skin and pink flesh completely.
Rinds from seedless varieties work well.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Remove outer green skin and inner pink flesh from watermelon rind. Cut rind into 1-inch cubes. Soak rind overnight in a lime solution (1 tablespoon calcium hydroxide or Mrs. Wages Pickling Lime per gallon of water) or in a brine of ¾ cup canning salt per gallon of water. Drain, rinse, and cover with fresh water; boil 30 minutes until just tender. Drain.
tips: Lime soak firms the rind for a crisper pickle.
Rinse thoroughly after lime soak — multiple rinses recommended.
Cook until just fork-tender; do not overcook.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Prepare syrup: combine 7 cups sugar, 2 cups white vinegar, 2 cups water, and spices (cinnamon sticks, cloves, allspice). Bring to a boil. Add rind cubes and simmer until rind appears translucent, about 30 to 45 minutes. Pack hot rind into hot pint jars. Pour boiling syrup over rind, leaving ½-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process pints 10 minutes (0–1,000 ft).
tips: Cook rind in syrup until translucent for best quality.
Pints: 10 minutes in boiling water bath.
Use whole spices tied in cheesecloth for cleaner appearance.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: At 1,001–3,000 ft: add 5 minutes. At 3,001–6,000 ft: add 10 minutes. Above 6,000 ft: add 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: About 8 to 9 pints from one large watermelon. Approximately 7 pounds of trimmed rind per canner load.
tips: Allow 2–4 weeks before tasting — flavor develops with time.

items.name: Ground or Chopped Meat
items.safety_notes: Use fresh, chilled meat. Remove excess fat before packing. Pressure canning required.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose fresh, chilled meat. For best results, use freshly ground, high-quality meat. Chill freshly ground or chopped meat to 40°F or below before canning.
tips: Keep meat refrigerated at 40°F or below until ready to can.
Grind or chop meat just before canning for best quality.
Use within 1–2 days of grinding if not canning immediately.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Choose fresh chilled meat. With beef, lamb, pork, and veal, remove excess fat. Sausage may be formed into patties or balls or left loose. Brown the ground or chopped meat in a skillet without adding extra fat to remove as much fat as possible. Season with salt, if desired. Fill jars loosely with pieces, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add boiling meat broth, tomato juice, or water, covering pieces and leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles and adjust headspace if needed.
tips: Brown meat thoroughly before packing — do not pack raw.
Drain off excess fat after browning.
Add 1 tsp canning salt per quart for flavor (optional).
Use boiling broth or water to cover; leave 1-inch headspace.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Fill hot jars loosely with pieces, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add boiling broth, tomato juice, or water, covering pieces and leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe jar rims. Adjust lids and process immediately.
tips: Remove air bubbles with a thin spatula before sealing.
Wipe rims with a clean damp cloth before applying lids.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Always adjust pressure for your altitude.
Use a dial-gauge canner above 2,000 ft for finer pressure control.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 1 pound of ground or chopped meat is needed per pint jar. Process times: pints — 75 minutes; quarts — 90 minutes (pressure canner only).
tips: Pints: 75 min; Quarts: 90 min — pressure canner only.
Do not attempt water-bath canning for any meat product.

items.name: Chicken or Turkey
items.safety_notes: Use fresh, chilled poultry. Remove excess fat and skin. Pressure canning required.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose freshly killed and dressed, healthy birds. Dressed chickens should be chilled for 6 to 12 hours before canning. Dressed turkeys should be chilled for 12 to 24 hours before canning. Reflectance canning is not recommended — do not use commercially frozen poultry that has not been thawed under refrigeration.
tips: Chill whole birds 6–24 hours before canning.
Keep poultry at 40°F or below until processing begins.
Use only fresh or properly thawed poultry.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Wash hands, work surfaces, and utensils thoroughly. Remove skin and fat from poultry pieces. Hot pack: boil, steam, or bake meat until about two-thirds done. Add 1 teaspoon salt per quart to the jar, if desired. Fill jars with pieces and hot broth, leaving 1¼-inch headspace. Raw pack: add 1 teaspoon salt per quart, if desired. Fill jars loosely with raw pieces, leaving 1¼-inch headspace. Do not add liquid.
tips: Remove skin before packing to reduce fat.
Bone-in pieces are acceptable; boneless also works well.
Hot pack gives better flavor and more meat per jar.
Raw pack — do not add liquid; the meat creates its own juices.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: For hot pack: fill jars with pieces and hot broth, leaving 1¼-inch headspace. For raw pack: fill jars loosely with raw pieces, leaving 1¼-inch headspace; do not add liquid. Remove air bubbles. Wipe jar rims with a dampened clean paper towel. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Leave exactly 1¼-inch headspace for poultry.
Remove all air bubbles before sealing.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Check your dial gauge annually for accuracy.
Add 5 lb weight pressure if above 1,000 ft with weighted gauge.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 3½ pounds of whole chicken yields 1 quart canned poultry. Process times: Without bones — pints 75 min, quarts 90 min. With bones — pints 65 min, quarts 75 min.
tips: Bone-in takes less time than boneless.
Quarts require longer processing than pints.

items.name: Fish (Tuna, Mackerel, etc.)
items.safety_notes: Use only fresh, high-quality fish. USDA recommends half-pint or pint jars only. Pressure canning required.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Only fresh fish should be canned. Fish must be bled, gutted, and chilled immediately after catching. Keep fish at 40°F or below. Process within 2 days of catching for best quality. Do not can fish that smell, look, or feel spoiled.
tips: Bleed fish immediately after catching.
Keep on ice (32–40°F) until ready to can.
Can within 48 hours for best safety and quality.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Clean and wash fish thoroughly. Remove head, tail, fins, and scales. Wash well and split fish lengthwise, if desired. Cut cleaned fish into 3½-inch lengths. Fill pint jars (do not use quarts), skin side next to glass, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1 teaspoon of salt per pint, if desired. Do not add liquids.
tips: Use only pint jars — quarts are not tested/approved for fish.
Place skin side against the glass for better appearance.
Salt is optional but adds flavor; use canning salt.
Do not add any water or oil — fish will produce its own liquid.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Fill jars, skin side next to glass, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1 teaspoon salt per pint, if desired. Do not add liquids. Remove air bubbles and adjust headspace if needed. Wipe jar rims with a dampened clean paper towel. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Do not add liquids of any kind.
Process at 10 lb pressure (0–1,000 ft): 100 minutes for pints.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Fish requires a full 100 minutes at pressure — do not shorten.
Always adjust pressure for altitude.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 1 pound of fresh fish per pint jar. Process pints only at 100 minutes. Quart jars are not recommended for fish.
tips: Pints only: 100 minutes processing time.
Expect some liquid separation — this is normal.

items.name: Beef, Pork, or Lamb (Strips or Cubes)
items.safety_notes: Use fresh, well-chilled meat. Remove excess fat. Do not use cured or smoked meat in these directions.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Choose high quality, chilled meat. Keep meat refrigerated at 40°F or below. Remove excess fat, gristle, and bruised spots. Soak strong-flavored game meats in brine water before canning if desired.
tips: Trim all visible fat — fat can cause off-flavors and sealing problems.
Remove gristle and connective tissue for better texture.
Game meat benefits from a 1-hour soak in salted water (1 tbsp/qt).

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Remove excess fat. Soak strong-flavored wild meats for 1 hour in brine water containing 1 tablespoon of salt per quart. Rinse. Remove large bones. Hot pack: precook meat until rare by roasting, stewing, or browning in a small amount of fat. Add 1 teaspoon of salt per quart, if desired. Fill jars with pieces and add boiling broth, drippings (with fat removed), water, or tomato juice, leaving 1-inch headspace. Raw pack: add 1 teaspoon of salt per quart, if desired. Fill jars with raw meat pieces, leaving 1-inch headspace. Do not add liquid.
tips: Hot pack: brown or roast until just rare before packing.
Raw pack: pack tightly — no liquid needed.
Remove as much fat as possible from drippings before adding.
Cut cubes uniformly (about 1–1½ inch) for even processing.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Hot pack: fill jars with pieces and add boiling broth, fat-free drippings, water, or tomato juice, leaving 1-inch headspace. Raw pack: fill jars with raw meat pieces, leaving 1-inch headspace; do not add liquid. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Process immediately.
tips: Wipe jar rims carefully — meat residue can prevent sealing.
Remove all air bubbles before lid application.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Dial-gauge canners must be checked annually for calibration.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 1 pound of boneless meat per pint jar. Process times: pints — 75 minutes; quarts — 90 minutes.
tips: Pints: 75 min; Quarts: 90 min at pressure.
Pressure canner only — water bath is never safe for meats.

items.name: Meat Stock and Broth
items.safety_notes: Skim off fat before canning. Cool broth and skim solidified fat. Use only tested USDA directions. Includes beef, chicken, turkey, and other poultry stocks.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only fresh, high-quality meat and bones. Chill bones and meat before preparing stock. Simmer cracked or cut bones in water for 3 to 4 hours. Remove bones, cool broth, and remove fat. Reheat to boiling and fill jars.
tips: Roast bones first for richer flavor.
Strain broth through cheesecloth for clarity.
Chill broth overnight and skim solidified fat before canning.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Simmer cracked or cut bones or meat scraps in water for 3 to 4 hours. Remove fat. Strain and season with salt to taste, if desired. Reheat broth to boiling and fill jars, leaving 1-inch headspace.
tips: Remove all visible fat before canning — fat causes rancidity.
Season lightly; over-salted broth cannot be corrected after canning.
Reheat to a full rolling boil before ladling into jars.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Reheat broth to boiling. Fill hot jars, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe jar rims with a dampened clean paper towel. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Fill jars while broth is at a rolling boil.
Leave 1-inch headspace exactly.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Always process broth in a pressure canner, never water bath.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: Yield varies by bone-to-water ratio. Process times: pints — 20 minutes; quarts — 25 minutes.
tips: Pints: 20 min; Quarts: 25 min at pressure.
Label jars with date and type of stock.

items.name: Clams, Minced
items.safety_notes: Use only very fresh live clams. Discard any with open or broken shells before processing. Seafood spoils rapidly — process immediately after preparation.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only live clams. Shell clams just before canning. Clams that do not close when tapped are dead and must be discarded. Keep live clams at 32–40°F until shucking.
tips: Tap shells — discard any that do not close.
Process as quickly as possible after harvest.
Clams must be alive when shucked.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Keep live clams cool until ready to can. Scrub shells. Place clams in steamer basket and steam until shells just open (5 to 10 minutes). Remove clam meat. Save clam liquor. Mince clam meat. Wash minced meat in water containing 1 teaspoon of salt per quart. Drain. Add ½ teaspoon of salt per pint jar, if desired.
tips: Steam only until shells open — do not overcook.
Rinse minced meat in lightly salted water to remove sand.
Strain reserved liquor through cheesecloth to remove grit.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Fill pint jars with minced clam meat, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add hot clam liquor, boiling water, or a combination to cover meat, leaving 1-inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Adjust lids and process. Use pint jars only.
tips: Pint jars only — quarts are not tested for minced clams.
Cover meat completely with hot liquor or water.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Seafood requires full pressure processing — no water bath.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 4 quarts of shell clams yields about 1 pint of minced clam meat. Process pints only: 60 minutes.
tips: Pints only: 60 minutes processing time.

items.name: Oysters
items.safety_notes: Use only very fresh live oysters. Raw pack only. Discard any with open shells. Process immediately — do not hold prepared oysters at room temperature.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only live, fresh oysters. Keep oysters cold (32–40°F) until processing. Discard any with open or broken shells. Process as quickly as possible after harvest.
tips: Harvest or purchase oysters the same day you plan to can.
Keep on ice until shucking.
Discard any dead (gaping shell) oysters.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Keep oysters cold until ready to can. Wash shells. Place oysters in a wire basket; submerge in boiling water for 5 minutes. Drain and open shells. Remove meat. Wash meat in water containing ½ cup of salt per gallon. Drain. Add ½ teaspoon of salt per pint jar, if desired.
tips: The 5-minute hot-water treatment makes shucking easier.
Rinse shucked meat in salted water to remove shell fragments.
Salt in brine wash is for cleaning, not preservation.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Pack oysters loosely into pint jars, leaving 1-inch headspace. Do not add liquid. Wipe rims. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Pint jars only — do not use quarts.
Do not add water or liquid.
Pack loosely — do not compress.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Pressure canning is mandatory for all shellfish.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 4½ pounds of oysters in the shell yields 1 pint canned. Process pints only: 75 minutes.
tips: Pints only: 75 minutes processing time.

items.name: Salmon
items.safety_notes: Use only fresh, high-quality salmon. Pint jars only — do not use quart or half-pint jars for this process. Skin and bones (softened by processing) are safe to eat.

sections.heading: Quality
sections.body: Use only fresh, high-quality salmon. Bleed, gut, and chill immediately after catching. Keep at 32–40°F. Process within 2 days of catching. Salmon with soft, mushy, or off-odor flesh should not be canned.
tips: Bleed immediately after catching for best color and flavor.
Keep on ice continuously until processing.
Can within 48 hours for best quality.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: Remove head, tail, fins, and scales. Wash and remove all blood. Split fish lengthwise. Cut into pint-jar-length pieces. Fill pint jars, skin side next to glass, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1 teaspoon of canning salt per pint, if desired. Bones are safe and softened by processing; they add calcium.
tips: Leave the backbone in — bones soften and become edible.
Place skin against glass for easier removal after opening.
Use canning or pickling salt, not table salt.
Do not add liquid — salmon produces its own.

sections.heading: Procedure
sections.body: Fill pint jars, skin side next to glass, leaving 1-inch headspace. Add 1 teaspoon salt per pint, if desired. Do not add liquid. Remove air bubbles. Wipe rims. Adjust lids and process.
tips: Pint jars only — quart jars are not tested/approved for salmon.
No liquid addition needed or desired.

sections.heading: Altitude Adjustments
sections.body: Process in a dial-gauge pressure canner: 0–2,000 ft — 11 lb; 2,001–4,000 ft — 12 lb; 4,001–6,000 ft — 13 lb; 6,001–8,000 ft — 14 lb. Process in a weighted-gauge pressure canner: 0–1,000 ft — 10 lb; above 1,000 ft — 15 lb.
tips: Never reduce processing time or pressure below the tested levels.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.body: An average of 1 pound of fish per pint jar. Process pints only: 100 minutes.
tips: Pints only: 100 minutes — do not cut this time short.
The long processing time ensures complete safety.
